cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The checked general-metric result remains 2+ε with a strict budget, while the classical hardness threshold is 1+2/e. The FPT algorithm, Euclidean schemes and 2026 k-Means results do not settle the polynomial-time target here.

context_blocks.text: Metric k-Median selects a limited number of service locations and minimizes total distance to the nearest selected location. The number of clients and the number of candidate facilities may differ, and the distance table need not come from a Euclidean embedding. The same formulation models representative selection for clustering and placement of facilities. Its simplicity makes the unresolved approximation threshold a central benchmark for algorithm design.

The two endpoint numbers are approximately 1.73576 and 2. The lower endpoint is the classical hardness threshold 1+2/e; the best general feasible guarantee in the checked literature is 2+ε. The inherited STOC 2025 paper explicitly asks for a tight approximation result after obtaining that upper bound. Asking for 1+2/e+ε for every fixed ε avoids requiring that an infimum approximation ratio be achieved exactly.

The coverage origin of the lower endpoint can be seen directly. Represent each set as a candidate facility and each universe element as a client. Give a client–facility pair distance one when the set contains the element and distance three otherwise, and give distinct pairs on the same side distance two. These distances satisfy the triangle inequality. A collection of k sets covering a fraction p of the elements then has clustering cost (3−2p) times the universe size.

Feige’s Max k-Cover gap distinguishes complete coverage from coverage of at most 1−1/e+η, for any fixed η>0. Under the preceding metric construction this becomes a gap between cost one per client and cost at least 1+2/e−2η per client. This is why the constant is not an arbitrary numerical target. A randomized algorithm beating that gap on every input would yield randomized algorithms for the underlying NP-hard decision problem; the appropriate exclusion is NP≠RP for this card’s success convention.

Jain–Mahdian–Saberi’s 2002 paper gives the classical metric k-Median lower bound through a reduction to approximating Set Cover. Its historical statement uses the then-known slightly-superpolynomial-time assumption for Set Cover hardness. The coverage reduction above explains the stronger ordinary NP-hardness formulation without silently changing the assumption in the original theorem. Neither lower-bound route excludes approximation from just above 1+2/e.

The 2025 algorithm combines two components. One permits a logarithmic number of extra centers while retaining a 2+ε cost bound; another handles instances where deleting one optimal center increases the optimum substantially. Combining them returns a feasible solution opening at most k centers. The full paper’s May 2026 revision retains this result. It is therefore incorrect to describe the headline 2+ε theorem as only a bicriteria approximation.

The usual linear relaxation has a separate barrier near two. It uses fractional openings y_s, assignments x_{c,s}≤y_s, unit total assignment for each client, and Σ_s y_s≤k. For a star with q≥3 leaves, all vertices available as facilities, clients at the leaves and k=q−1, every integral optimum has cost two. Set the central opening to 1/(q−1), each leaf opening to (q−2)/(q−1), and assign each client’s remaining fraction to the center. This feasible LP solution costs q/(q−1), giving an integrality gap approaching two.

That explicit example limits a guarantee measured against this relaxation, not every polynomial algorithm measured against OPT. A sharper algorithm might use additional constraints, a different relaxation, or another method. Likewise, a lower bound for one rounding framework is not a computational impossibility theorem for the original optimization problem. The card’s target is deliberately stated using the true integral optimum.

There is already a matching-threshold algorithm in a different runtime regime. Cohen-Addad–Gupta–Kumar–Lee–Li’s ICALP 2019 work achieves 1+2/e+ε in fixed-parameter time with respect to k. The potentially large dependence on the number of opened facilities is permitted there. This does not supply a polynomial-time algorithm when k grows as part of the input, but it shows that the target ratio has meaningful algorithmic support.

A 2026 development concerns geometric input. Cohen-Addad and coauthors improve approximation-scheme runtimes in low-dimensional Euclidean spaces, where additional structure is available. Such a scheme does not apply to arbitrary distance tables.

Anand and coauthors’ July 2026 spectral dual-fitting paper improves k-Means guarantees, including in general metrics. That objective sums squared distances; squaring changes both the analysis and the hardness constants. It does not establish the stated k-Median ratio.

Resolving this question would determine whether the coverage obstruction captures the full cost of efficient metric clustering. A positive answer would bridge the remaining gap beyond the familiar LP benchmark. A stronger hardness threshold would reveal an obstruction not expressed by coverage alone. The exact facility budget is essential to either conclusion: averaging an excessive number of facilities over random choices changes the feasible problem.

cards.title: A constant improvement over factor two for Vertex Cover
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Do a constant ε∈(0,1) and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm exist which, on every finite simple undirected graph G, output a vertex cover of size at most (2−ε)τ(G)?
cards.definitions: Use uniform classical deterministic Turing computation, with no advice or oracle. Integers and rational numerators and denominators are encoded in binary; L denotes the total input bit length. A polynomial bound has constants independent of the input. A vertex cover is a subset S of the vertices containing at least one endpoint of every edge; τ(G) is the minimum size of such a set. The graph is represented by its adjacency matrix. The same ε and algorithm must work for graphs of all sizes, with no promise on degree, coloring or graph class. An edgeless input requires the empty cover. The question asks for an unconditional algorithm or unconditional refutation of its existence.

context_blocks.text: Vertex Cover is one of the canonical NP-hard covering problems and has a simple factor-two approximation. The absence of a fixed improvement despite extensive work makes the factor a central approximation barrier.

Unique Games implies hardness below two, while unconditional NP-hardness leaves a gap. A restricted graph-class algorithm does not answer the universal target. The source seminar situates the question in the development of approximation algorithms and primal-dual methods.

cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.

sentences: Does the minimum directed traveling-salesman tour always cost at most twice the subtour LP optimum?
The LP allows fractional arcs but imposes one incoming and outgoing unit at every vertex and a cut condition for every proper vertex set.
Known examples approach factor two, whereas the 2024 book proves a general upper bound of seventeen.
The June 2026 finite half-integral computations do not cover all fractional solutions or all sizes.
A resolution would identify the strength or a failure of this central relaxation for asymmetric routing.

upgraded_from.title: The factor-2 integrality-gap conjecture for the ATSP subtour LP

references.title: Research reference · epubs.siam.org

cards.definitions: A directed metric is a function c:V×V→R≥0 with c(i,i)=0 and c(i,k)≤c(i,j)+c(j,k) for all i,j,k. Symmetry is not required, and distinct vertices may have zero distance. The complete directed graph has one arc (i,j) for each i≠j and no loops. A Hamiltonian cycle visits every vertex once before returning to its start; its cost is the sum of its n arc costs. OPT_ATSP(c) is the minimum over all such cycles. For S⊆V, δ⁺(S)={(i,j):i∈S,j∉S} and δ⁻(S)={(i,j):i∉S,j∈S}; for a set of arcs F write x(F)=Σ_(i,j)∈F x_ij. LP_ATSP(c) minimizes Σ_i≠j c(i,j)x_ij over real variables x_ij≥0 subject to x(δ⁺({v}))=x(δ⁻({v}))=1 for every v, and x(δ⁺(S))≥1 for every nonempty proper S⊊V. The degree equalities imply x(δ⁺(S))=x(δ⁻(S)), so an additional incoming-cut inequality would be redundant. No integrality restriction is placed on x. The feasible set is nonempty and compact; both optima are attained. The inequality, rather than division by LP_ATSP(c), also covers zero-cost instances. For positive LP value, the integrality ratio is OPT_ATSP(c)/LP_ATSP(c), and the overall gap is its supremum over all n and directed metrics. The question is a universal comparison of optimum values, without a running-time restriction on finding the tour. It concerns closed tours, not a prescribed-start/end path.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed factor-2 inequality for every finite directed metric and every size, or exhibit a finite directed metric with a rigorously proved strict violation. An affirmative answer need not attain ratio 2 on a finite instance: known families approach 2. An approximation algorithm proved only relative to the true tour optimum, or a result restricted to a subset of LP extreme points, does not establish the universal LP inequality.

context_blocks.title: Buying fractions of directed arcs
context_blocks.text: A tour buys each used arc completely. The relaxation permits fractional amounts of several arcs, while requiring one unit to enter and leave every city and at least one unit to leave every proper group of cities. Every tour is feasible for the LP, so the LP gives a lower bound on the tour cost. The question asks whether converting the best fractional cost into an actual tour ever entails a factor larger than two. A fractional solution need not be a probability distribution over whole tours.

context_blocks.title: Why subtour constraints matter
context_blocks.text: Suppose six cities form two groups of three, with travel cost 1 within a group and 10 between groups. Two separate three-city directed cycles satisfy every degree condition and cost only 6, but do not form a tour visiting all cities. The cut inequality for either group rules out this disconnected solution. These inequalities therefore add a global requirement to the local degree constraints; whether that requirement is strong enough to keep the full gap at two is the unresolved issue.

context_blocks.title: The current general gap
context_blocks.text: Families of directed instances have ratios tending to 2, so no smaller universal factor can work. Traub and Vygen’s 2022 article establishes an upper bound of 22. Their 2024 book improves the proved bound to 17 and explicitly retains the factor-2 question. Its circulation LP has the same optimum as the degree-constrained LP on directed metrics, so the model matches this card. The book also notes room for a small further numerical improvement; 17 is a stated theorem, not a claim that no refinement exists.

context_blocks.title: Finite computations and half-integral vertices
context_blocks.text: Vercesi and coauthors construct improved lower-bound instances at particular sizes. The June 2026 revision by Sosso, Bernardelli and Gualandi computes the gaps for all half-integral extreme points through twelve vertices, where half-integral means coordinates in {0,1/2,1}. An extreme point is a feasible LP solution that cannot be written as a nontrivial convex combination of two distinct feasible solutions. Other denominators and arbitrarily large instances remain outside that enumeration. These computations add evidence without proving the universal conjecture.

context_blocks.title: What a resolution would establish
context_blocks.text: The comparison measures the strength of this specific relaxation. A polynomial-time method achieving cost at most twice the LP optimum would settle the inequality and give an approximation guarantee, but the existence inequality itself does not promise an efficient construction. The symmetric metric TSP has a different classical 4/3 conjecture; its constants and finite verifications do not transfer to the larger family in which travel costs can depend on direction.

cards.title: Constant-factor approximation for uniform Sparsest Cut
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Do a universal C≥1 and a randomized polynomial-time algorithm exist which, on every finite simple undirected graph G on n≥2 vertices, output a nonempty proper set S with φ_G(S)≤C min_{∅≠T⊊V} φ_G(T), with probability at least 2/3?
cards.definitions: Here φ_G(S)=|E(S,V∖S)|/(|S|·|V∖S|), where E(S,V∖S) is the set of edges having exactly one endpoint in S. The graph is supplied explicitly by an adjacency matrix. Polynomial time is measured in bit operations on every random tape; the same algorithm and constant must work for all graphs. The zero-optimum disconnected case requires returning a zero cut. Uniform refers to equal demand for each pair of vertices, not regularity of the graph.

context_blocks.text: Uniform Sparsest Cut balances a cut’s edge boundary against the number of separated pairs. It is a basic measure of the decomposability of a graph and a major test case for approximation algorithms.

The ARV result gives an O(√log n) approximation, with a bound growing with the graph size. A constant factor would cross the remaining qualitative approximation barrier. Nonuniform pair demands, conductance normalized by volumes, and Small-Set Expansion have different targets and are not silently substituted here.

cards.why: Determine whether a central graph-decomposition objective admits approximation independent of instance size.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.

cards.title: Unconditional NP-hardness at the Goemans–Williamson Max-Cut threshold
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: For every rational ε with 0<ε<1−α_GW, do rationals 0<b<a≤1 with b/a<α_GW+ε exist such that distinguishing Max-Cut value at least a from value at most b is NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions?
cards.definitions: For a finite simple undirected graph with at least one edge, its Max-Cut value is the maximum fraction of edges crossing a bipartition. Let α_GW=min_{0<θ≤π} 2θ/(π(1−cos θ)). NP-hardness means there is a polynomial-time map from 3-CNF formulas to graphs mapping satisfiable formulas to the at-least-a case and unsatisfiable formulas to the at-most-b case. The reduction and constants may depend on ε. No Unique Games or other hardness conjecture is assumed.

context_blocks.text: The Goemans–Williamson approximation ratio is a landmark in semidefinite optimization. Matching hardness from ordinary NP-hardness would identify that ratio as an intrinsic computational threshold under P≠NP.

Known optimal hardness follows from Unique Games; it is not an unconditional NP-hardness theorem. The target deliberately concerns the reduction itself, so a conditional implication from UGC does not count as a solution. This separates the problem from the Unique Games conjecture and from improving a particular rounding algorithm.

cards.title: The deterministic k-server conjecture
cards.formal: For every integer k≥1, every metric space (M,d) with at least k+1 points, and every initial placement C_0 of k servers, does there exist a deterministic online serving rule A and a finite constant β≥0 such that cost_A(σ;C_0)≤k·OPT(σ;C_0)+β for every finite request sequence σ∈M*? The rule and β may depend on M,d,k,C_0, but neither may depend on future requests or on the length of the request sequence.
cards.definitions: The metric is symmetric, has finite real distances, is zero exactly on equal points, and satisfies the triangle inequality; the space may be finite or infinite and is known to the online rule. There are exactly k interchangeable, unweighted servers, whose current positions form a multiset. A request r_t must be served before r_{t+1} is revealed. If a server is already at r_t, no movement is needed; otherwise the rule chooses one of the k servers and moves it to r_t, paying the metric distance. Restriction to these lazy moves loses no competitive power. A deterministic online rule is a function of the known metric, initial placement and revealed request prefix, with arbitrary memory and no access to future requests; this card imposes no running-time bound. OPT is the minimum total movement cost of an offline rule serving the same finite sequence from C_0 with the same k servers and advance knowledge of the sequence. The additive β must be fixed before requests arrive and cannot grow with the number or cost of requests. Randomization, advice about future requests, and extra servers are not supplied.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A central problem in competitive analysis that asks whether the number of available servers exactly captures the worst-case price of future uncertainty. Its techniques and limitations inform caching, online movement and broader metric optimization problems.

importance.reason: A foundational conjecture about online decision-making, with an optimal lower bound, one broadly applicable candidate algorithm, and a persistent gap on general metrics despite many resolved special cases.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The April 2026 primary source retains the deterministic conjecture and the general (2k−1) upper bound. The 2023 randomized disproof concerns O(log k), not the deterministic factor k. This card fixes all finite request sequences, identical initial placements, exactly k servers and an additive constant independent of requests; it asks for any deterministic online rule, not specifically WFA.

context_blocks.text: The problem isolates the price of making placement decisions without seeing future demand. Servers can represent cache slots, mobile resources or copies of data; a movement pays for changing which demand locations are covered. On a uniform metric, where every distinct pair has distance one, serving a request is precisely the paging problem. The online rule and the offline optimum have the same number of servers. Their difference is information about the future, not available capacity.

The proposed factor k is a sharp target, already forced by paging lower bounds. The classical work of Manasse, McGeoch and Sleator establishes the lower-bound framework and settles the two-server case on general metrics. An additive constant is included so that a fixed initial placement does not distort asymptotic performance. Allowing that constant to depend on the request sequence would make the definition vacuous, which is why its quantifiers are explicit.

Koutsoupias and Papadimitriou prove that the work-function algorithm is (2k−1)-competitive on every metric space. Its work function records the minimum offline cost of serving the already revealed prefix and ending in each possible server configuration. The algorithm uses these values to weigh movement against how well a configuration fits the past. This provides a single general strategy and leaves a factor approaching two between the known guarantee and the conjectured optimum.

It is widely conjectured that the same algorithm is actually k-competitive. Proving that stronger statement would settle this card, but the card permits a completely different algorithm. Similarly, failure of one proposed potential function only identifies a gap in that proof method. A potential proof typically compares changes in a quantity assigned to the current work function with the online and offline costs, so that the inequalities telescope over an arbitrarily long request sequence.

Several geometric settings attain the target. Chrobak and Larmore give k-competitive algorithms on tree metrics, covering line-like settings as well. Trees have unique connecting paths, which support movement rules unavailable in arbitrary metrics. This is substantial positive evidence, but arbitrary metric spaces can contain cycles and distance patterns that do not admit the same analysis.

Huang and Zhang prove that the work-function algorithm is 3-competitive on a circle, with distance measured along the shorter circular arc. Their result first appeared in a 2022 preprint and was published in Theoretical Computer Science in 2024. They also give computer-assisted evidence excluding their defined canonical family of potential functions for the general three-server case. The geometric theorem and the limitation of that proof family are different conclusions.

Bubeck, Coester and Rabani’s STOC 2023 theorem disproves the randomized O(log k) conjecture by constructing metrics with randomized competitive ratio Ω(log²k). It does not refute the deterministic target k: these are different claimed rates, and log²k is asymptotically smaller than k. The deterministic lower bound and the (2k−1) upper bound remain the relevant endpoints here.

Brilliantov, Bamas and Abbé’s April 2026 benchmark studies automated searches for potentials, particularly for four servers on a circle. A violated checked inequality refutes a candidate under the chosen formulation, while passing the finite checks is not a proof for every metric configuration and request sequence. Their experiments leave the open case unresolved. This offers concrete research tooling without changing the status of the conjecture.

cards.title: A constant improvement over factor 2 for unrelated-machine makespan
cards.formal: Does there exist a constant ε with 0<ε<1 and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm which, for every unrelated-machine scheduling instance, assigns all jobs to machines with makespan at most (2−ε)OPT?
cards.definitions: An instance consists of m≥1 machines, n≥0 independent jobs, and an explicitly given m×n matrix of processing times pᵢⱼ in the nonnegative rationals or ∞. Rational numerators and denominators are binary encoded; ∞ forbids an assignment. Every job has at least one finite processing time. A schedule is a function σ:{1,…,n}→{1,…,m} with p_{σ(j),j}<∞. Its makespan is Cmax(σ)=maxᵢ Σ_{j:σ(j)=i} pᵢⱼ, and OPT is the minimum of this quantity over all feasible schedules. Jobs are available at time zero, indivisible and processed without interruption on one machine; there are no precedence constraints or communication costs. Jobs assigned to one machine can run consecutively in any order. The algorithm must output σ, not merely an estimate of OPT. Its bit running time is polynomial in the entire input length. ε and the polynomial are independent of m, n and all processing times; no predictions or promises on matrix structure are supplied. Empty or zero-optimum instances require makespan zero. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A defining unresolved approximation barrier in scheduling. Beating two by any fixed constant would also imply a constant approximation for general Santa Claus allocation, while known relaxation gaps rule out a large family of straightforward proofs.

importance.reason: A decades-old central scheduling problem with a large hardness gap, robust LP barriers and formal consequences for fair allocation.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The full worst-case constant-improvement question remains open in the checked primary literature. The known 2−1/m ratio and prediction-assisted results have different quantifiers from the fixed-ε target. The 3/2 hardness is conditional on P≠NP.

context_blocks.text: Each job can have a completely different processing time on each machine. There need not be a single ranking from fastest to slowest machines, as in the related-machine model. The challenge is to balance total load while respecting which assignments are expensive or forbidden. Even when every job has an individually attractive machine, sending all jobs to their favorite machines can create a severe bottleneck.

Lenstra, Shmoys and Tardos obtain a polynomial-time factor-2 approximation by rounding a fractional assignment. For a candidate makespan T, assignments with pᵢⱼ>T are forbidden; the relaxation divides each job fractionally among the remaining machines while bounding each machine’s fractional load by T. Their rounding can charge the overload to at most one additional job per machine. Since every eligible job fits individually within T, the resulting schedule has load at most 2T.

The same foundational work establishes NP-hardness of approximation below 3/2. This leaves a genuine gap: the known hardness is compatible with an algorithm of ratio 1.9, 1.75 or 1.5. Moreover, Shchepin and Vakhania improve the general guarantee to 2−1/m. That is strictly less than two for each finite number of machines, but it approaches two as m grows. The ε in this question must be one fixed positive constant, so this refinement is not a resolution.

A stronger relaxation uses configurations: a variable represents an entire subset of jobs that fits on one machine within T. This remembers much more local packing structure than individual fractional assignments. Nevertheless, Verschae and Wiese construct an integrality gap approaching two even when each job is eligible on at most two machines. Thus rounding this relaxation solely against its own optimum cannot prove a universal constant improvement. This is a limitation of the relaxation, not a hardness theorem for all algorithms.

Restricted assignment is a special case in which job j has one processing time pⱼ on all eligible machines. It is substantially more structured than arbitrary unrelated processing times. Bamas and coauthors obtain a polynomial-time (1.75+δ)-approximation for the further restriction to two finite job sizes. Their general two-value unrelated-machine result instead gives 2−1/nᵟ for fixed δ>0, whose improvement still depends on instance size. Neither guarantee extends to the full target here.

The same SODA 2024 paper gives a formal connection to the Santa Claus allocation problem, where indivisible resources must be distributed to maximize the least satisfied player’s additive value. A (2−1/α)-approximation for makespan, for constant α≥2, would yield an (α+δ)-approximation for general Santa Claus for any fixed δ>0. Thus even a small fixed improvement here would also resolve a major constant-factor approximation question in fair allocation.

Baba, Bampis and Mitropoulos’ June 2026 preprint studies predictions of assignments for heavy jobs. For accurate predictions their algorithm approaches factor one, while its worst-case guarantee with arbitrary prediction error remains two. This identifies valuable information that helps scheduling, but the classical question supplies no such information. A worst-case proof cannot assume that a learned assignment resembles an optimal schedule.

The fundamental issue is whether indivisibility forces an approximation barrier at two, or whether a stronger global argument can control the interactions that fractional rounding loses. Progress would clarify both the power of optimization relaxations and the complexity of balancing heterogeneous resources.

cards.title: Breaking factor two for precedence-constrained makespan
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant ε∈(0,1) and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, for every instance of P|prec|Cmax with an input number m of identical parallel machines, produces a feasible nonpreemptive schedule of makespan at most (2−ε)OPT?
cards.definitions: An input specifies n≥1 jobs, a positive integer processing time p_j for each job, a directed acyclic graph of precedence constraints, and a positive integer machine count m. All numbers are encoded in binary and the graph is given explicitly. The machine count is not fixed in advance; one may cap it at n because additional machines cannot help. A feasible schedule chooses a machine a_j∈{1,…,m} and a nonnegative start time s_j for every job. Job j occupies that machine continuously during [s_j,s_j+p_j), without preemption or migration. Intervals assigned to the same machine must be disjoint. For every precedence edge i→j, require s_j≥s_i+p_i. Every job can run on every machine and its processing time is independent of the chosen machine. There are no release dates, deadlines, communication delays, setup costs or extra resource constraints. The makespan is Cmax=max_j(s_j+p_j); OPT is the minimum over feasible schedules using the same m unit-speed machines. With integer processing times, an optimal schedule with integer start times exists, so the algorithm can output binary-encoded integer starts. Polynomial time is measured in the full input bit length, not in Σ_j p_j. The same fixed ε must apply for all n, all m, all processing times and all precedence DAGs. The algorithm receives the whole instance before constructing the schedule.
cards.answer_criterion: Give one such fixed ε and prove a polynomial-time (2−ε) guarantee for all inputs, or rule out every fixed improvement below two with any complexity assumptions explicitly stated. A bound 2−1/m does not supply a universal ε. Guarantees for fixed m, unit jobs only, special precedence orders, quasipolynomial running time, extra machines or faster processors do not prove the requested statement. A conditional hardness result based on a stronger conjecture must remain labelled conditional.
cards.why: Determine whether arbitrary precedence constraints allow a constant improvement over the classical factor-two makespan guarantee on identical machines.

references.authors: Venkatesan Guruswami; Xuandi Ren; Shaoxuan Tang

cards.status_note: No polynomial-time fixed (2−ε) improvement found through 11 September 2026. Svensson’s factor-two hardness requires the specified possibly stronger Unique Games variant. Recent fixed-machine approximation schemes and exact unit-job algorithms have narrower scope, while July 2026 UMPS hardness imposes machine eligibility restrictions absent here.

context_blocks.text: Two basic obstructions limit how quickly dependent jobs can finish. Total work W=Σ_j p_j needs at least W/m time across m machines. A precedence chain must execute sequentially, so the length L of a longest weighted path is another lower bound. A schedule must manage both parallel throughput and the timely completion of jobs that unlock later work. Even with identical machines and no communication costs, these priorities can conflict.

Graham’s list scheduling follows a fixed priority order and starts available jobs whenever machines become free. A job is available once all its predecessors have finished. Its analysis gives Cmax≤W/m+(1−1/m)L, and hence Cmax≤(2−1/m)OPT. The bound approaches two as the machine count grows. Therefore the fact that each individual instance has a guarantee strictly below two does not resolve the constant improvement in this question.

A simple example shows why choosing priorities matters. Take m(m−1) independent unit jobs and one independent job of length m. If the long job comes last in the list, the units occupy all machines for m−1 time, and the final job finishes at 2m−1. An optimal schedule starts the long job immediately and runs the unit jobs on the other m−1 machines, finishing at time m. This proves a limitation of that list order, not hardness for every algorithm: the example has no precedence edges.

Classical NP-hardness excludes approximation factors below 4/3 unless P=NP, leaving room between that barrier and two. Svensson’s STOC 2010 work, published in 2011, connects the missing hardness to a different scheduling objective: minimizing total weighted completion time on one machine with precedences. Sufficiently strong hardness near factor two for that problem transfers to makespan on identical parallel machines, even with unit processing times.

Combined with Bansal and Khot’s hypothesis, the reduction gives hardness for every fixed factor below two. The hypothesis is a particular Unique Games variant with additional structure: near-perfect satisfiability on large subsets in the yes case and an expansion requirement in the no case. Svensson explicitly describes it as possibly stronger than the usual Unique Games conjecture. Thus this is substantial conditional evidence, but it should not be presented as a theorem following solely from P≠NP.

There has been strong progress when the number of machines is a fixed constant and jobs have unit length. Levey–Rothvoss initiate a line of approximation schemes based on hierarchy relaxations, followed by faster bounds. Das and Wiese provide a simpler quasipolynomial scheme by guessing selected jobs and time intervals and filling the remaining positions greedily. Their paper was published at ESA 2022, despite being uploaded to arXiv in January 2025. Its fixed-machine and running-time restrictions are essential.

Nederlof, Swennenhuis and Węgrzycki advance exact algorithms for unit jobs. Their bound (1+n/m)^{O(√(nm))} is subexponential when m=o(n), and they also give an exponential improvement when m is proportional to n. The work appeared at SODA 2025 and was published online in ACM Transactions on Algorithms in January 2026. Exactness is stronger than approximation, but these running times are not polynomial and the processing-time promise remains narrower than this card’s model.

Guruswami, Ren and Tang’s July 2026 preprint proves that even unit-length jobs can be hard to approximate within any constant when each job has one predetermined eligible machine. That extra restriction prevents the scheduler from freely distributing ready jobs. It is a different model, called unique-machine precedence scheduling, and its hardness transfers to certain communication-delay models. It does not contradict the factor-two guarantee available when every job may use any identical machine.

A fixed improvement below two would show that global information about the precedence graph can reliably overcome the worst interactions between chain length and machine utilization. A matching hardness theorem under a standard assumption would explain why a very old greedy guarantee remains near the limit of efficient scheduling. The question isolates that issue without combining it with heterogeneous machines, strategic reports, or communication delays.

cards.title: Constant additive error for one-dimensional bin packing
cards.formal: Do a universal integer C≥0 and a randomized polynomial-time algorithm exist that pack every explicitly listed one-dimensional bin-packing instance into at most OPT+C unit-capacity bins with probability at least 2/3?
cards.definitions: The input is a list of n≥1 rational item sizes s₁,…,s_n∈(0,1], each encoded as a binary numerator and positive binary denominator; L is the total encoding length. A feasible packing is a map b:[n]→[k] with Σ_{i:b(i)=j}s_i≤1 for every bin j. OPT is the minimum feasible integer k. The algorithm is uniform and classical, has access to the entire input before assigning items, and must output an explicit feasible packing. For absolute constants K,d, every execution must take at most KL^d bit operations. Its output is always feasible, and on each fixed input it uses at most OPT+C bins with probability at least 2/3 over its private random bits. C,K,d are independent of n, the number of distinct sizes, OPT and coefficient precision. No capacity augmentation, splitting of items, cardinality constraint or promise on the input distribution is allowed. Repeated items are explicitly listed rather than represented by binary multiplicities. Randomization is expressly allowed; a deterministic algorithm would also resolve the question. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A basic boundary between asymptotic approximation and almost exact combinatorial optimization: can efficient packing lose only a fixed number of bins on every instance?

importance.reason: A longstanding central problem in approximation algorithms, with connections to configuration LPs, discrepancy and the computational effect of input encoding.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No universal constant-additive polynomial-time algorithm or general impossibility result was found in the checked primary sources. context_blocks.text: The objective is to minimize the number of identical containers needed to hold indivisible items. Each bin has a single numerical capacity constraint, so the model contains no geometric placement issue. Nevertheless, many different combinations of small and large items can fit exactly or almost exactly, and choices that look locally efficient can leave unusable capacity elsewhere. The inherited invited survey explicitly asks for an OPT+O(1) guarantee.

Additive and multiplicative errors behave differently as the optimum grows. A one-percent excess can mean thousands of unnecessary bins on a large instance; an additive constant remains fixed. Conversely, this card allows any universal constant, even a very large one. It does not ask for an additive-one algorithm or for exact optimization on small instances.

The elementary hardness example is distinguishing instances needing two bins from those needing three, through Partition. This rules out exact polynomial optimization under the usual complexity assumptions, but it does not settle constant additive approximation. With allowance C=1, a valid three-bin answer is permitted in both cases. A stronger hardness argument would need a gap that survives the particular additive allowance.

Asymptotic approximation schemes achieve a ratio approaching one, with additional losses depending on their accuracy parameter. This does not automatically give OPT+C. Choosing ε on the order of 1/OPT makes ε·OPT small, but the additive term and the running time may worsen as ε shrinks. The dependence on every parameter must be controlled simultaneously; the existence of a scheme alone does not establish the desired fixed loss.

Several published bounds use the Gilmore–Gomory configuration LP. A configuration specifies a multiset of item types that fits in one bin. The LP permits fractional numbers of such bins while covering all required items. Its optimum OPT_f is a lower bound on the integral optimum. Karmarkar–Karp obtain a polynomial-time packing with O(log² OPT) additive loss by combining approximate LP optimization with repeated rounding.

Hoberg–Rothvoss improve the guarantee to OPT_f+O(log OPT_f), and hence OPT+O(log OPT). Their Theorem 2 gives randomized expected polynomial time in the number of explicitly represented items, with the usual accounting for encoded numerical data. Packing first into intermediate containers, and then into bins, improves how rounding errors accumulate. This is the logarithmic-additive general algorithmic benchmark found in the checked literature.

A constant additive LP integrality gap is a related mathematical conjecture, but it is not identical to this card. An efficiently constructible packing within a constant of OPT_f would suffice. A nonconstructive proof of a small gap would still need an algorithmic rounding step. Conversely, an unbounded gap for this LP would not rule out a different algorithm whose guarantee is measured against the true integral optimum.

Discrepancy results explain why several familiar approaches encounter barriers. Eisenbrand–Pálvölgyi–Rothvoß connect a restricted bin-packing relaxation to discrepancy of three permutations. Their revised paper also proves limitations for a class of algorithms based on rounding item sizes upward. Those limitations concern specified techniques, rather than all algorithms for the original packing problem.

Newman–Nikolov disprove the conjecture that three permutations always have constant discrepancy, constructing examples requiring Ω(log n). This eliminates one proposed route to a constant additive bound. It does not itself provide numerical item sizes with a growing bin-packing integrality gap, and it does not show that every polynomial-time packing algorithm must lose logarithmically many bins.

Recent work also settles nearby structural questions. Jansen–Pirotton–Tutas’s ESA 2025 paper constructs bin-packing instances requiring exponentially many distinct configurations as a function of the number of item types. Its discussion records an OPT+1 algorithm whose runtime depends heavily on that parameter. Exponential support in the number of types does not contradict a polynomial algorithm in an explicit list of all items, and a parameter-dependent additive-one algorithm is not uniformly polynomial as the number of types grows.

The ICALP 2026 work of Jansen–Ohnesorge–Pirotton proves a tight ETH-based lower bound for the dependence on the number of types in a high-multiplicity exact algorithmic regime. Binary multiplicities can encode far more items than the input length. Both the compressed input model and exact optimization differ from the constant-additive, explicitly listed target here. The result should therefore not be reported as a negative answer to this question.

This problem isolates how close efficient approximation can come to an integral packing optimum. A constant-additive algorithm would show that all unavoidable combinatorial inefficiency can be confined to a bounded number of extra bins, regardless of instance size. A general impossibility theorem would establish a meaningful approximation barrier beyond the standard two-versus-three-bin hardness example.

Karmarkar–Karp obtain a polynomial-time packing with O(log² OPT) additive loss by combining approximate LP optimization with repeated rounding.

Hoberg–Rothvoss improve the guarantee to OPT_f+O(log OPT_f), and hence OPT+O(log OPT). Their Theorem 2 gives randomized expected polynomial time in the number of explicitly represented items, with the usual accounting for encoded numerical data. Packing first into intermediate containers, and then into bins, improves how rounding errors accumulate. This is the logarithmic-additive general algorithmic benchmark found in the checked literature.

A constant additive LP integrality gap is a related mathematical conjecture, but it is not identical to this card. An efficiently constructible packing within a constant of OPT_f would suffice. A nonconstructive proof of a small gap would still need an algorithmic rounding step. Conversely, an unbounded gap for this LP would not rule out a different algorithm whose guarantee is measured against the true integral optimum.

Discrepancy results explain why several familiar approaches encounter barriers. Eisenbrand–Pálvölgyi–Rothvoß connect a restricted bin-packing relaxation to discrepancy of three permutations. Their revised paper also proves limitations for a class of algorithms based on rounding item sizes upward. Those limitations concern specified techniques, rather than all algorithms for the original packing problem.

Newman–Nikolov disprove the conjecture that three permutations always have constant discrepancy, constructing examples requiring Ω(log n). This eliminates one proposed route to a constant additive bound. It does not itself provide numerical item sizes with a growing bin-packing integrality gap, and it does not show that every polynomial-time packing algorithm must lose logarithmically many bins.

Recent work also settles nearby structural questions. Jansen–Pirotton–Tutas’s ESA 2025 paper constructs bin-packing instances requiring exponentially many distinct configurations as a function of the number of item types. Its discussion records an OPT+1 algorithm whose runtime depends heavily on that parameter. Exponential support in the number of types does not contradict a polynomial algorithm in an explicit list of all items, and a parameter-dependent additive-one algorithm is not uniformly polynomial as the number of types grows.

The ICALP 2026 work of Jansen–Ohnesorge–Pirotton proves a tight ETH-based lower bound for the dependence on the number of types in a high-multiplicity exact algorithmic regime. Binary multiplicities can encode far more items than the input length. Both the compressed input model and exact optimization differ from the constant-additive, explicitly listed target here. The result should therefore not be reported as a negative answer to this question.

This problem isolates how close efficient approximation can come to an integral packing optimum. A constant-additive algorithm would show that all unavoidable combinatorial inefficiency can be confined to a bounded number of extra bins, regardless of instance size. A general impossibility theorem would establish a meaningful approximation barrier beyond the standard two-versus-three-bin hardness example.

cards.definitions: Let d,T≥1 be integers and B₂^d={x∈R^d:Σ_i x_i²≤1}. A permitted constraint set K is a compact convex subset of R^d satisfying B₂^d⊆K⊆dB₂^d; the learner knows K,d,T in advance. This is an affine normalization of general full-dimensional convex bodies, not a smoothness condition on losses. Write F(K) for the Borel-measurable convex functions f:K→[0,1], where convexity means f(λx+(1−λ)y)≤λf(x)+(1−λ)f(y) for x,y∈K and λ∈[0,1]. No common Lipschitz, differentiability, strong-convexity or curvature bound is imposed. Before any play, an oblivious adversary fixes f₁,…,f_T∈F(K), possibly using knowledge of the learner’s policy but not its realized random choices. At round t the learner chooses X_t∈K, incurs f_t(X_t), and observes exactly that one real value. It receives no noise, gradient, second evaluation, whole function or future loss. A policy is a sequence of Borel probability kernels assigning a distribution on K to each observed history (X₁,f₁(X₁),…,X_(t−1),f_(t−1)(X_(t−1))). This permits arbitrary randomized decision rules; computation, representation and sampling time are unrestricted, so the target is statistical rather than polynomial-time optimization. For fixed K, define R_K(T)=inf_π sup_(f₁,…,f_T) E_π[Σ_t f_t(X_t)−inf_(x∈K)Σ_t f_t(x)], with the supremum over fixed legal loss sequences and expectation only over policy randomness. Finally R*(d,T)=sup_K R_K(T), over the normalized bodies above. The comparator is one fixed point for all rounds, chosen in hindsight. Using an infimum avoids assuming a minimizer on the boundary. Joint constant-factor precision means a stated function g(d,T) and universal constants a,b>0 with a g(d,T)≤R*(d,T)≤b g(d,T) for all d,T≥1. Constants cannot depend on the shape of K. The Borel convention ensures the displayed expectations are defined.
cards.answer_criterion: Identify a joint rate g(d,T) and prove upper and lower bounds within universal constant factors for the defined minimax value. The upper bound must hold for every allowed convex body and loss sequence with some admissible policy for that known body; the matching lower bound must hold against every policy on suitable allowed instances. Bounds for a fixed dimension with unspecified dimension-dependent constants, or bounds that hide an unresolved polynomial or logarithmic factor, do not give the full requested rate. Efficient implementation is not an additional acceptance condition.

context_blocks.title: One value does not reveal a direction
context_blocks.text: On the interval [−1,1], the convex losses f(x)=(1+x)/2 and h(x)=(1−x)/2 both equal 1/2 at x=0, but their minimizing endpoints are opposite. Observing one loss value therefore need not reveal which way to move. Across rounds the loss may also change, so a value observed yesterday is not a second evaluation of today’s function.

context_blocks.title: The benchmark is one fixed decision in hindsight
context_blocks.text: Regret compares accumulated loss with the best single point that could have been used throughout the sequence. It does not compare with a different minimizer on every round. This distinction makes learning possible even when the environment changes. Randomization protects the learner against a sequence chosen before its random actions, while the adversary may still choose that sequence with knowledge of the policy.

context_blocks.title: Dimension remains a major gap
context_blocks.text: Lattimore’s 2020 theorem gives an upper bound of order d^(5/2)√T, apart from a logarithmic factor, for exact one-point feedback. In the regime where T is sufficiently large relative to d, known lower bounds grow as d√T. The March 2026 book explicitly retains the dimension gap. For smaller horizons, regret is always at most T because each loss lies in [0,1]; an asymptotic expression must respect this saturation.

context_blocks.title: Normalization and computational cost
context_blocks.text: Bounded loss values fix the scale of regret. Restricting K to a rounded affine position prevents an arbitrary choice of coordinates from introducing an extra geometric parameter. This still permits general convex losses and many domain shapes. The information-theoretic question asks what is attainable by decision rules with no computation limit. A practical algorithm can be a major advance while still having a worse dimension dependence than the best existence bound.

context_blocks.title: Which newer results change the assumptions
context_blocks.text: The July 2026 revision of Ye’s paper uses two evaluations per loss and assumes strong convexity, with carefully stated comparator guarantees. Cheng, Hatano and Takimoto’s June 2026 result allows globally budgeted perturbations but assumes a smooth convex underlying loss even when the perturbations vanish. These assumptions differ from arbitrary bounded convex functions with one exact observation. Neither establishes the minimax rate requested here.

cards.title: A constant-competitive algorithm for the general matroid secretary problem
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant C≥1 such that every finite matroid M admits a randomized online selection strategy which, for every assignment of nonnegative weights to its elements, returns an independent set of expected weight at least OPT(M,w)/C when the elements arrive in a uniformly random order?
cards.definitions: A matroid is a finite set E and a nonempty family I⊆2^E closed under subsets and satisfying augmentation: if A,B∈I and |A|<|B|, some b∈B∖A has A∪{b}∈I. The strategy knows E and I in advance, but not the weights. A fixed adversary assigns w:E→ℝ_{≥0} before the order and strategy coins are sampled. Upon each arrival its identity and weight are revealed. The strategy must accept or reject it irrevocably before the next arrival, keeping the accepted set in I. OPT(M,w)=max_{S∈I}∑_{e∈S}w(e). Expectation includes a uniformly random permutation of E and the strategy’s independent random coins. There is no computation or oracle-query bound; this is the competitive-existence conjecture for the full-information matroid model.

context_blocks.text: The general matroid secretary problem asks whether random arrival order is enough to recover a constant fraction of a best feasible weighted set without seeing future weights. It unifies classical secretary selection with broad independence constraints.
The random-assignment model also randomizes where weights are placed, and admits stronger results. Those results do not settle the adversarial-assignment, random-arrival model used here.

cards.why: The main unresolved competitive-ratio question for online selection under general matroid constraints.

cards.title: A polylogarithmic randomized competitive ratio for k-server on every metric
cards.formal: Do universal constants C,a>0 exist such that, for every integer k≥2, finite metric space (X,d) with |X|≥k+1, and initial placement of k servers, a randomized online strategy has expected total movement cost at most C(1+log₂k)^a OPT(σ)+β on every finite request sequence σ? The additive constant β may depend on the metric, k and initial placement, but not on σ or its length.
cards.definitions: There are k movable servers at points of X; repeated server locations are allowed. Each request names a point of X. Before the next request, at least one server must occupy that point. Moving a server from u to v costs d(u,v). The full finite metric and initial placement are known. OPT(σ) is the minimum total movement of a strategy knowing the entire sequence and starting at the same placement. The adversary is oblivious: it fixes σ independently of the online strategy’s random coins. The strategy uses only the prefix revealed so far. No running-time bound is imposed. The exponent a and multiplicative constant C must be independent of |X|, k and the metric.

context_blocks.text: Randomized k-server is a central test of whether an online algorithm can manage a large changing state at a cost depending mildly on the number of servers. The number of metric points must not occur in the competitive ratio.
The old O(log k) conjecture is false: a superlogarithmic lower bound is known. Polylogarithmic dependence on k remains a different open target. Bounds containing log|X| do not settle it.

cards.title: The minimax rate of sequential binary calibration
cards.formal: Determine C(T)=inf_A sup_B E[∑_{p∈P_A}|∑_{t:p_t=p}(y_t−p)|] up to universal multiplicative constants as the integer horizon T tends to infinity, in the finite-forecast sequential game below. The requested rate includes logarithmic factors.
cards.definitions: Before play, forecaster A selects a finite set P_A⊆[0,1], which may depend on T. Both players know this set and T. At each time t, A selects p_t∈P_A and adversary B selects y_t∈{0,1} simultaneously; neither sees the other’s current selection. Each may randomize using independent coins and the full history (p_s,y_s)_{s<t}, and after the round both selections become public. The infimum is over every such finite set and randomized forecaster, and the supremum is over all randomized adaptive adversaries. There is no computational restriction. The displayed sum measures unnormalized ℓ₁ calibration error and is finite; groups are defined by exact equality of predictions. Expectation is over both players’ coins.

context_blocks.text: Calibration asks whether forecasts agree with empirical frequencies on the rounds when each probability was announced. The minimax rate measures the unavoidable error in this requirement against an adaptive sequence of binary events.

The long-standing T^{2/3} upper bound has already been improved by a constant in the exponent. A lower bound strictly above √T is also known. Thus neither the old two-thirds barrier nor a square-root target is an appropriate new open question. The remaining problem is the optimal rate itself.

cards.title: Planted clique: can polynomial time detect a clique below the square-root scale?
cards.formal: Is the following hardness statement true? For every fixed ε∈(0,1/2), there is no uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm A whose success probability in the experiment below is at least 2/3 for every sufficiently large n, with k=⌊n^(1/2−ε)⌋.
cards.definitions: Set [n]={1,…,n}. The null distribution N_n draws a simple undirected labeled graph by including each unordered pair independently with probability 1/2. The planted distribution P_(n,k) first chooses S uniformly among all k-element subsets of [n], includes all edges inside S, and includes every other edge independently with probability 1/2. Draw b uniformly from {0,1}; draw G from N_n if b=0 and P_(n,k) if b=1. Give A the binary integers n,k and the full adjacency matrix of G, but neither b nor S. It outputs a bit b̂. Success means Pr[b̂=b], averaged over b, the graph, S when present, and A’s independent random bits. Equivalently success is (Pr_N[A=0]+Pr_P[A=1])/2. Polynomial time means at most C(n+1)^c bit operations for every input and random tape, with fixed C,c; they and A may depend on the fixed ε. The forbidden guarantee is ∃A,C,c,N ∀n≥N, success≥2/3. This is a one-graph detection problem; A may generate its own random graphs at its own computational cost. The size of S is exactly k, not an independent per-vertex planting probability. No advice, quantum computation, oracle, side information, or algorithm-family restriction is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A foundational average-case hardness hypothesis and a central test case for statistical–computational gaps. It asks for a clean separation between the presence of information and efficient extraction of that information; reductions transfer related assumptions to sparse estimation and latent-structure learning. Proving this formulation would in particular imply P≠NP, since a polynomial algorithm for maximum clique would distinguish the distributions.

importance.reason: A canonical computational threshold with broad consequences in average-case complexity, statistical inference, and the study of algorithmic lower-bound frameworks.

progress.text: Alon, Krivelevich, and Sudakov give polynomial-time recovery for k≥c√n for any fixed c>0, using spectral methods and boosting.

Barak, Hopkins, Kelner, Kothari, Moitra, and Potechin prove a nearly tight sum-of-squares integrality gap: degree d=o(log n) assigns random graphs clique value n^(1/2−o(1)). This is a restricted-model lower bound.

Gheissari, Jagannath, and Xu show that an appropriate discrete gradient descent and low-temperature local chain recover at the √n scale from the full-graph initialization; the final preprint version is dated 15 May 2025.
Nagda and Raghavendra derive optimal efficient distinguishing advantages conditional on a planted-clique hypothesis, in the independent-vertex planting model.

Göbel, Ruff, and Schiller give robust sum-of-squares algorithms for multiple overlapping cliques in random intersection graphs when clique size is much larger than √(n log n). This is progress in a related model, not below the threshold fixed here.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026; no unrestricted polynomial-time solution below n^(1/2−ε) or unconditional hardness proof was identified. The exact formulation fixes constant-success detection and exactly k planted vertices. Low-degree and sum-of-squares bounds remain scoped to their models; the optimal-advantage result is conditional.

context_blocks.text: This asks whether a planted structure can be statistically obvious yet computationally inaccessible. In the specified regime, k grows as a positive power of n, while an unplanted graph has no clique of size r=⌈3 log_2 n⌉ with probability tending to one: a union bound is at most n^r·2^(−r(r−1)/2), which tends to zero. Enumerating all r-subsets therefore distinguishes the two distributions with success tending to one in quasipolynomial time n^O(log n). The obstacle is reducing that computation to polynomial time, not a lack of information in the graph.

The classical spectral algorithm of Alon, Krivelevich, and Sudakov recovers the hidden vertex set for every fixed positive constant times √n, with a polynomial whose exponent can depend on that constant. Recovery immediately yields detection here by checking that the reported set is a sufficiently large clique. Letting the constant shrink as n^(−ε) does not keep that analysis polynomial with a fixed exponent.

Substantial evidence comes from provable failures of general algorithmic frameworks. Barak and coauthors show that low-degree sum-of-squares relaxations assign a random graph an implausibly large clique value near √n, despite its true largest clique having only logarithmic size. This is an unconditional limitation of that relaxation. It does not rule out every algorithm allowed in this card.

Recent positive work also illustrates why an algorithmic barrier must state its model. Gheissari, Jagannath, and Xu permit local optimization to pass through vertex sets that are not cliques, penalizing missing edges. Starting from the whole graph, their procedure reaches the planted clique at a sufficiently large constant times √n. Restrictions to moves among actual cliques can fail even in easier regimes; those failures do not establish the unrestricted conjecture.

Nagda and Raghavendra obtain sharp bounds on efficient distinguishing advantage assuming planted-clique hardness. Their paper uses independent vertex planting, so the planted size fluctuates around its mean, and uses a different normalization of advantage. It strengthens consequences of a hypothesis in that related model. It is not an unconditional lower bound for the fixed-size experiment here.

The question isolates detection from stronger output requirements such as recovering every planted vertex. It also fixes the random background: arbitrary base graphs, geometric random graphs, and adversarially modified edges describe different experiments. Work on robust recovery of overlapping planted cliques in random intersection graphs continued in COLT 2026, but its distribution and signal regime do not settle this question.

cards.title: Does P≠NP imply a samplable NP problem outside AvgP?
cards.formal: Is the implication $\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\Longrightarrow(\mathrm{NP},\mathrm{PSamp})\nsubseteq\mathrm{AvgP}$ true? That is, assuming P≠NP, must there exist a language L∈NP and a polynomial-time samplable distribution ensemble D={Dₙ} such that no deterministic exact decider for L runs in average polynomial time under D, in the moment-based sense defined below?
cards.definitions: A sampler is one randomized Turing machine S which, given 1ⁿ, halts within q(n) steps on every random tape for a fixed polynomial q. Its output distribution Dₙ is over finite binary strings x; |x|≤q(n), and n is the ensemble parameter, not necessarily |x|. Sampling is exact with independent unbiased coin flips, and S has no advice or oracle. An exact decider A receives (1ⁿ,x), halts, and returns the membership bit of L correctly for every n and x. Write T_A(1ⁿ,x) for its running time. The pair (L,D) belongs to AvgP if there exist such an A, ε>0, C>0, and integer k≥1 with $\mathbb E_{x\sim D_n}[T_A(1^n,x)^\varepsilon]\le C(n+1)^k$ for every n≥1. The constants and A may depend on L and S but not on n. This moment definition is the robust Levin notion, not the requirement that the first moment itself be polynomial. The algorithm is deterministic and never gives a wrong answer; difficult inputs may take a long time. NP uses ordinary polynomially bounded certificates and deterministic polynomial-time verification. Both the hard language and its sampler must be fixed across all input lengths.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This asks whether worst-case intractability necessarily survives on inputs generated by a feasible process. It is the basic bridge between the standard theory of NP-completeness and distributional complexity, and a prerequisite issue in attempts to derive useful cryptographic hardness from P≠NP alone.

importance.reason: One of the central missing implications in complexity theory, connecting worst-case lower bounds to feasible instance generation and the limits of algorithms on typical inputs.

progress.text: Levin develops robust average-time definitions and distributional completeness; Impagliazzo and Levin extend completeness to samplable ensembles. The survey develops the moment definition and this completeness theory.

Bogdanov and Trevisan show limitations of nonadaptive worst-case-to-average-case oracle reductions for NP. Their result is a conditional obstruction to a reduction method, not a disproof of the unrestricted implication.
Wigderson’s Open Problem 4.5 and the revised Bogdanov–Trevisan survey explicitly ask whether P≠NP implies average-case NP hardness.

Liu and Pass obtain a worst-case-to-average-case reduction for an exact time-bounded Kolmogorov problem under an exponential circuit-hardness derandomization assumption. The extra hypothesis is stronger and more specific than P≠NP.

cards.status_note: The original question is explicitly open in Wigderson’s book and the revised average-case survey. Current primary literature was checked through 10 September 2026; no resolution from P≠NP alone was located. The card fixes deterministic exact AvgP and strict polynomial-time sampling, rather than conflating them with randomized heuristic hardness.

context_blocks.text: Worst-case hardness says that an algorithm has difficult inputs. It does not say that a feasible instance generator produces them with enough probability to obstruct average efficiency. The sampler is therefore part of the mathematical problem. It may depend on the language, but it cannot contain an uncomputable table selecting a hard input at every length.

A padding example shows why a fixed familiar distribution is insufficient. Encode a formula x as 0 followed by |x|²−1 further zeros, a separator 1, and x. Satisfiability of these padded strings remains NP-complete under polynomial reductions. Under the uniform distribution on strings of a fixed length, valid encodings are so rare that checking the format and brute-forcing the rare valid formulas has polynomial average cost. An easy uniform distribution does not remove worst-case hardness.

Levin’s moment condition makes average efficiency stable under polynomial slowdowns. If a machine is simulated with its running time raised to a fixed power, a correspondingly smaller positive moment still suffices. This prevents the answer from depending on an incidental choice of machine representation. Exact computation with this runtime guarantee differs from a heuristic allowed to give incorrect answers on a small fraction of inputs.

Distributional completeness is already available: Impagliazzo and Levin extend the theory to polynomial-time samplable ensembles. Completeness identifies a common average-case target; it does not prove that this target is hard from P≠NP.

There are barriers for nonadaptive oracle reductions from worst-case NP hardness to average-case NP hardness: the relevant reductions would collapse the polynomial hierarchy. Such a barrier leaves other proof mechanisms open. Recent reductions for specific time-bounded Kolmogorov problems use additional assumptions or specific forms of hardness, so they do not supply the implication on this card.

cards.title: The computational threshold for dense tensor PCA
cards.formal: For every fixed integer k≥3, rational ε with 0<ε<(k−2)/4, and rational c∈(0,1), is the following impossibility statement true? No uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm, given the finite-precision observation of Y=n^{k/4−ε}v^{⊗k}+Z specified below, achieves |⟨u,v⟩|≥c with probability at least 2/3 for every sufficiently large dimension n, where v is uniform on the unit sphere in R^n and the n^k ordered entries of Z are independent N(0,1) variables.
cards.definitions: The experiment draws v, Z and the algorithm’s random bits independently. For an ordered tuple (i₁,…,i_k)∈{1,…,n}^k, the signal entry is n^{k/4−ε}v_{i₁}⋯v_{i_k}. Noise is not pre-symmetrized and each entry has variance one. To give polynomial time a precise bit-model meaning, for n≥2 set b=⌈10k log₂n⌉ and Q_b(x)=2^{−b}⌊2^b max(−2^b,min(x,2^b))⌋. The input consists of n and all entries Q_b(Y_{i₁,…,i_k}), represented as signed dyadic rationals with O(log n) bits each. This fixed rounding convention is an explicit finite-precision version of the usual Gaussian-model question. An algorithm may depend on the fixed constants k, ε and c, but is one probabilistic Turing machine for all n, with worst-case running time polynomial in n on every input and random tape. For fixed k this is polynomial in the input size. It outputs a nonzero rational vector w, interpreted as the unit vector u=w/‖w‖₂; zero or invalid outputs fail. Success is the event |⟨w,v⟩|≥c‖w‖₂. The algorithm receives no side information about v, informative initial vector, or additional independent observations. The probability averages over the spike, noise and internal randomness. Absolute correlation makes the target invariant under the unavoidable sign ambiguity when k is even.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that for every fixed (k,ε,c) in the stated ranges, each such polynomial-time algorithm has success probability below 2/3 for arbitrarily large n; or refute this by giving one fixed triple and one algorithm that succeeds with probability at least 2/3 for all sufficiently large n. Proving failure only for low-degree polynomials, a chosen iterative method, or a different spike prior does not prove the full assertion. An improvement by logarithmic factors at n^{k/4} does not supply the fixed power saving n^ε requested here.
cards.why: Determine whether the canonical statistical–computational gap for a dense Gaussian tensor persists against all polynomial-time recovery algorithms.

importance.reason: A central average-case inference problem linking tensor algorithms, statistical thresholds, low-degree methods and computational hardness.

progress.text: Montanari–Richard introduce and analyze the spiked tensor model, exhibiting a gap between information-theoretic recovery and the analyzed polynomial-time methods.
Kunisky–Moore–Wein prove spherical-prior low-degree detection thresholds and odd-order reconstruction lower bounds with the predicted dependence on degree.
Wu–Zhou sharpen the analysis and stopping rule for randomly initialized power iteration; its threshold improves by a polylogarithmic factor.

cards.status_note: The May 2026 low-degree paper retains the conjectured gap for unrestricted algorithms and distinguishes spherical from independent-coordinate priors. The 2024 power-iteration and October 2025 stochastic-gradient improvements concern particular methods and do not provide a fixed-power improvement below n^{k/4}. No full resolution found through 11 September 2026. The card explicitly fixes a finite-precision bit model; restricted lower bounds in the standard unrounded model are evidence, not a proof for all algorithms here.

context_blocks.text: Ordinary principal component analysis looks for a hidden direction in a noisy matrix. Tensor PCA asks the analogous question when observations have three or more indices. Here the clean signal has rank one: every entry is a product of coordinates of the same hidden unit vector. Gaussian noise obscures those products. The goal is only a constant correlation with the direction, much weaker than estimating every coordinate accurately.

For fixed tensor order, information-theoretic recovery in the standard Gaussian model becomes possible at a signal scale of order √n. Montanari and Richard established the basic statistical-versus-computational distinction while studying tensor unfolding, power iteration and message-passing methods. Their noise normalization differs from the variance-one convention used in this card; their constant statistical threshold corresponds to order √n here.

Known polynomial-time methods reach signal strength around n^{k/4}, up to factors that do not change this leading exponent. Wu and Zhou’s 2024 introduction records both this algorithmic scale and the conjectured gap from √n. The interval for ε deliberately places our target strictly between them: λ/√n=n^{(k−2)/4−ε} grows without bound. There is therefore ample statistical signal in the usual model, while efficient recovery remains unproved.

For example, at order four and ε=1/8, the observation contains n^4 noisy numbers and signal strength n^{7/8}. The statistical scale is n^{1/2}, and the conjectured efficient scale is n. A polynomial-time algorithm below that latter scale would have to exploit structure that current threshold evidence misses. Merely reading all n^4 entries is allowed: the question concerns computation polynomial in the complete input, not a sublinear-access restriction.

Low-degree polynomial estimators provide one rigorous way to test proposed computational barriers. Kunisky, Moore and Wein establish the predicted degree-versus-signal tradeoff for detection with a spherical spike and derive a matching reconstruction lower bound for odd tensor orders. Their reconstruction theorem is specifically for odd orders; they explain that even orders require a sign-invariant estimand such as vvᵀ and additional work. Detection and recovery are separate tasks, and a detection lower bound should not silently be relabelled as their reconstruction theorem.

Fu and Sohn’s May 2026 preprint advances low-degree estimation bounds for tensor PCA with independent, mean-zero, variance-one spike coordinates and bounded moments. Its general-prior theorem controls estimation of fixed products of coordinates and obtains the predicted signal-versus-degree scaling within a stated degree range. Independent-coordinate priors are different from a vector conditioned to have unit norm. The result strengthens evidence for the computational gap without establishing an unrestricted polynomial-time lower bound for this card’s spherical prior.

Some recent algorithmic improvements resolve narrower conjectures. Wu and Zhou lower the threshold for randomly initialized power iteration by a polylogarithmic factor. Ding, Gu, Liu and Fang obtain improved guarantees for an overparameterized stochastic-gradient method using multiple independent observations. For even order, their stated sample-signal condition reaches the familiar n^{k/4} scale after averaging the observations. Neither result supplies the fixed-power improvement below that scale demanded here.

The rounding convention prevents an ambiguity about algorithms operating on exact Gaussian real numbers. Each coordinate is given with logarithmically many bits. Outside the clipping event, the total rounding error in Euclidean norm across the tensor is at most n^{k/2}2^{−b}, an extremely small inverse power of n; clipping has vanishing probability. This is a specified computational model, rather than an assertion that every exact-real algorithm automatically transfers to it. Likewise, polynomial-estimator theorems for unrounded observations do not by themselves cover arbitrary algorithms that process rounded entries.

A resolution would clarify whether a simple, highly symmetric random model can hide statistically recoverable information from every efficient algorithm. A successful method would challenge a widely used picture of algorithmic thresholds. A full impossibility proof would require a complexity argument beyond the restricted algorithm families currently understood. Both outcomes would inform how computational hardness assumptions are formulated for inference problems.

cards.title: The computational Kesten–Stigum threshold for sparse community recovery
cards.formal: Do there exist a fixed integer q≥5, fixed rational constants a>b>0 satisfying (a−b)²<q(a+(q−1)b), a constant δ>0, and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm A such that, for every sufficiently large n, A weakly recovers the communities of the symmetric stochastic block model SBM(n,q,a,b), with expected overlap at least 1/q+δ?
cards.definitions: Generate the hidden labels σ₁,…,σₙ independently and uniformly from [q]={1,…,q}. Conditional on these labels, each unordered pair of distinct vertices is independently an edge with probability a/n if its labels agree and b/n otherwise. Thus the graph is simple and undirected; take n≥a. Equal prior probabilities make communities asymptotically balanced, but their sizes are not conditioned to equal n/q. The algorithm receives this one graph and knows q,a,b; it receives no planted labels or auxiliary samples. It outputs a label vector σ̂∈[q]ⁿ. Define overlap(σ̂,σ)=max over permutations π of [q] of n⁻¹Σᵢ 1{σ̂ᵢ=π(σᵢ)}. The expectation in the question is over labels, graph edges and the algorithm’s random bits. Weak recovery means a fixed positive advantage over the limiting chance baseline 1/q. Running time is worst-case polynomial in n on a standard bit model, for every graph and random tape; the algorithm and polynomial exponent may depend on the fixed parameters but not on n. Put d=(a+(q−1)b)/q and θ=(a−b)/(a+(q−1)b). The strict inequality is dθ²<1, below the Kesten–Stigum threshold. All three model parameters remain constant as n grows.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer must exhibit one fixed parameter choice below the threshold and prove the stated polynomial running time and nonvanishing expected overlap for all sufficiently large n.
