cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No polylogarithmic-update algorithm meeting the fixed-accuracy, explicit-matching target was found. Matching-size estimators, ordered-RS-dependent bounds and the 2026 maximal-matching improvement do not resolve it.

context_blocks.text: A maximum matching allocates the largest possible number of disjoint pairs. When an edge changes, recomputing it from scratch ignores the substantial information retained from the preceding graph. The dynamic problem asks how much of that information can be reused while keeping a solution within an arbitrarily small fixed relative loss of optimum. Both insertions and deletions are allowed, so previously useful structure can disappear.

The graph’s optimum changes by at most one after a single edge update, but a particular solution may require coordinated replacements. On a long alternating path, gaining one additional matched edge can involve changing many pairs. Approximation creates room to postpone or distribute some repairs. The difficulty is to do so without accumulating a large loss or spending too much time discovering the repairs that are needed.

An explicit solution is part of the target. A number close to ν(G) need not identify even one edge that can safely be used with the others. A mate array makes this distinction observable: a query at a vertex must return its current partner or report that it is unmatched. Requiring the whole array to be printed after every update would impose an artificial linear output cost, so the formulation instead charges only actual changes and queries.

Maximality is also weaker than near-optimality. In a four-vertex path, selecting only the middle edge gives a maximal matching of size one, while the two outside edges give a maximum matching of size two. Randomized maximal-matching algorithms already achieve very small update times against oblivious sequences. Chuzhoy–Khanna–Song’s STOC 2026 result improves deterministic maximal matching to n^{1/2+o(1)} amortized time; its guarantee still concerns maximality.

A separate sequence of breakthroughs beats the factor-two barrier for estimating matching size in polylogarithmic update time. Azarmehr–Behnezhad–Roghani’s SODA 2024 result obtains an estimate corresponding to a 2−√2−η fraction of optimum in general graphs, for fixed η>0. The paper explicitly studies size estimation. Its title alone can therefore suggest a stronger maintenance result than the theorem actually supplies.

For maintaining actual near-optimal matchings, Assadi–Khanna–Kiss’s SODA 2025 work develops a connection to ordered Ruzsa–Szemerédi graphs. Such a graph has its edges partitioned into matchings, with each matching induced in the union of itself and later matchings. Dense examples quantify how often certain expensive matching searches can recur. Their update bound is expressed through this extremal quantity and works even against adaptive adversaries.

The dependence is roughly n^{o(1)} times the ordered-RS count for matchings of linear size, with accuracy-dependent parameters. A strong enough combinatorial upper bound would yield subpolynomial update time. This does not currently establish polylogarithmic time: n^{o(1)} can grow faster than every fixed power of log n, and the required extremal bounds are themselves unresolved. This connection is not an unconditional lower bound.

Pratt’s SOSA 2026 note relates the ordered and ordinary RS notions at the level of polynomial exponents. Dense ordered examples would imply nearly comparably dense ordinary examples. It resolves a structural question about the reduction’s graph families, but does not determine the density needed for a polylogarithmic dynamic algorithm.

Liu’s 2024 work gives a different advance for bipartite graphs: amortized update time n/2^{Ω(√log n)} times a polynomial in 1/ε. It also relates stronger update bounds to online matrix-vector problems. The dependence on accuracy is essential in those statements. In particular, the ordinary-OMv equivalence stated for approximate vertex cover should not be silently transferred to matching, and a barrier using inverse-polynomial accuracy does not settle this card’s fixed-ε question.

The adversary convention leaves useful flexibility. An oblivious sequence may be carefully chosen to be difficult, but it cannot react to random decisions or the current matching. The algorithm nevertheless receives updates one at a time; knowing that the sequence was fixed does not give access to future deletions. Similarly, amortization permits occasional expensive repairs as long as their expected total cost satisfies the bound.

The inherited Max Planck report explicitly identifies near-optimal fully dynamic matching with polylogarithmic updates as a long-term target. Its page 123 also distinguishes maintaining matching edges from estimating their number, and describes faster progress in the insertion-only setting. Allowing deletion of a vertex, which removes all its incident edges together, does not automatically supply an algorithm for arbitrary individual edge deletions.

The fundamental issue is whether a changing combinatorial optimum can be tracked almost as cheaply as the graph itself is updated. A positive result would close a major gap between coarse approximation and near-optimal explicit solutions. It would also clarify how much global matching structure must be recomputed when each input change is local.

cards.title: Polylogarithmic worst-case updates for exact dynamic minimum spanning forests
cards.formal: Can an exact minimum spanning forest of a fully dynamic n-vertex graph with polynomially bounded integer weights be maintained with polylogarithmic worst-case time per edge update, polynomial preprocessing and space, and high-probability correctness against an oblivious adversary?
cards.definitions: The graph is simple and undirected on the fixed labelled vertex set [n], n≥2, and starts empty. An update inserts one currently absent edge with integer weight in {1,…,n⁴}, or deletes one present edge. Edge weights remain fixed until deletion. A minimum spanning forest consists of one minimum-total-weight spanning tree for each connected component. Break equal-weight ties by the fixed lexicographic order (weight, smaller endpoint, larger endpoint), so the target is the unique forest selected by Kruskal’s algorithm in that order. After each update the data structure must report the edges removed from and added to the maintained forest; on a correct execution at most one edge of each kind changes. These reports specify the entire current forest starting from the empty one. Use a uniform randomized classical word RAM with Θ(log n)-bit words, standard word operations and random-word generation; all input processing and memory accesses count. For every fixed pair of integers a,b≥1, the target permits a separately tuned uniform data structure and constants K,C≥1 whose preprocessing and space are n^{O(1)}, and for which every update takes at most K(log₂(n+2))^C steps on every execution. For every valid update sequence of length at most n^a fixed before its random choices, all reported forests must be correct simultaneously with probability at least 1−n^{−b}. Constants and polynomial exponents may depend on a,b, but not on n or the sequence. This is a Monte Carlo worst-case-time formulation; an always-correct deterministic solution would also suffice. The integer range n⁴ is an explicit specialization, and weights occupy O(1) words. There is no advance access to future updates.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct data structures satisfying the stated bounds for every fixed a,b, or prove the proposition false. Amortized polylogarithmic updates, merely subpolynomial worst-case updates, or maintaining an approximate minimum forest are insufficient. A lower bound against deterministic algorithms alone does not rule out the allowed randomization. A data structure that only stores the graph and postpones finding the forest to an expensive query does not meet the required per-update reporting guarantee.
cards.why: A basic dynamic optimization problem with very small changes to its answer but potentially expensive global replacement searches. It tests whether amortized efficiency can be made reliable for every update.

importance.reason: One of the main unresolved worst-case update barriers in dynamic graph algorithms, closely connecting connectivity, weighted optimization, sparsification and expander maintenance.

Nanongkai–Saranurak–Wulff-Nilsen give Las Vegas subpolynomial worst-case update time with high probability.
Chuzhoy and coauthors obtain deterministic n^{o(1)} worst-case updates via deterministic expander decomposition.
Meierhans–Probst Gutenberg’s SODA paper gives expected polylogarithmic worst-case connectivity maintenance; its weighted extension is (1+ε)-approximate with inverse-ε overhead.

context_blocks.text: One edge update can force a global search even though the optimal forest changes by very little. Deleting a tree edge splits one tree into two parts; the algorithm must find the cheapest surviving edge crossing that cut, if one exists. There may be many candidate edges dispersed throughout the graph. Inserting an edge is easier to understand: it creates a cycle if its endpoints are already connected, and it replaces the largest edge on that cycle when this improves the ordered forest.

The reporting convention makes the maintained answer observable without requiring the algorithm to print all n−1 tree edges after every update. With fixed tie-breaking, the forest changes by at most one insertion and one deletion. Holm, Rotenberg and Wulff-Nilsen use this explicit update model in their formulation. The difficulty is finding those few changes quickly, rather than paying for a large unavoidable output.

Polylogarithmic amortized maintenance is already established. Holm, de Lichtenberg and Thorup give a deterministic O(log⁴ n) amortized update bound. Amortization allows occasional expensive operations as long as their cost can be charged across a sequence. The present target limits the time of each individual update, so long rebuilds and large replacement-edge searches must be spread out while keeping the current answer ready.

Later amortized refinements improve the logarithmic factors. The 2015 work of Holm, Rotenberg and Wulff-Nilsen obtains O(log⁴ n/log log n) using the randomized priority-queue option in its table of RAM implementations. Its deterministic implementation has a different bound. None of these variants supplies the worst-case per-update guarantee requested here.

The worst-case frontier crossed a major threshold in 2017. Nanongkai, Saranurak and Wulff-Nilsen obtain Las Vegas maintenance with subpolynomial worst-case update time with high probability. Their approach combines expander maintenance with a reduction to graphs having few edges beyond a forest. Chuzhoy and coauthors subsequently derandomize the needed expander-decomposition component and obtain deterministic n^{o(1)} worst-case updates.

Subpolynomial is still weaker than polylogarithmic. For example, exp(√log n) grows more slowly than every fixed positive power of n but faster than every fixed power of log n. Thus a statement of n^{o(1)} update time does not automatically meet this card’s bound. The 2020 deterministic theorem resolves an earlier polynomial-exponent barrier while leaving the sharper target.

The SODA 2026 connectivity result of Meierhans and Probst Gutenberg achieves expected polylogarithmic worst-case updates for maintaining an unweighted spanning forest, and also discusses conversion to high-probability time bounds. It extends to a (1+ε)-approximate weighted minimum spanning forest with overhead proportional to log(U)/ε for weights in [1,U]. The approximation parameter is essential; this is not an exact weighted minimum-forest theorem.

For integer weights, one could force an approximation guarantee to become exact by taking ε smaller than the reciprocal of a polynomial upper bound on the optimum cost. But the displayed 1/ε overhead would then become polynomial in n. The straightforward reduction therefore does not preserve polylogarithmic update time for exact optimization. It identifies a concrete gap between maintaining connectivity at a few approximate weight thresholds and identifying the exact cheapest replacement edge.

The oblivious-adversary convention means the update sequence is chosen without reacting to the data structure’s random outcomes. A solution robust to an adaptive adversary would be stronger. Even this stated convention would remove a longstanding delay barrier for a central dynamic optimization primitive, with uses in algorithms that repeatedly maintain weighted spanning structures.

cards.context:
One edge update can force a global search even though the optimal forest changes by very little. Deleting a tree edge splits one tree into two parts; the algorithm must find the cheapest surviving edge crossing that cut, if one exists. There may be many candidate edges dispersed throughout the graph. Inserting an edge is easier to understand: it creates a cycle if its endpoints are already connected, and it replaces the largest edge on that cycle when this improves the ordered forest.

The reporting convention makes the maintained answer observable without requiring the algorithm to print all n−1 tree edges after every update. With fixed tie-breaking, the forest changes by at most one insertion and one deletion. Holm, Rotenberg and Wulff-Nilsen use this explicit update model in their formulation. The difficulty is finding those few changes quickly, rather than paying for a large unavoidable output.

Polylogarithmic amortized maintenance is already established. Holm, de Lichtenberg and Thorup give a deterministic O(log⁴ n) amortized update bound. Amortization allows occasional expensive operations as long as their cost can be charged across a sequence. The present target limits the time of each individual update, so long rebuilds and large replacement-edge searches must be spread out while keeping the current answer ready.

Later amortized refinements improve the logarithmic factors. The 2015 work of Holm, Rotenberg and Wulff-Nilsen obtains O(log⁴ n/log log n) using the randomized priority-queue option in its table of RAM implementations. Its deterministic implementation has a different bound. None of these variants supplies the worst-case per-update guarantee requested here.

The worst-case frontier crossed a major threshold in 2017. Nanongkai, Saranurak and Wulff-Nilsen obtain Las Vegas maintenance with subpolynomial worst-case update time with high probability. Their approach combines expander maintenance with a reduction to graphs having few edges beyond a forest. Chuzhoy and coauthors subsequently derandomize the needed expander-decomposition component and obtain deterministic n^{o(1)} worst-case updates.

Subpolynomial is still weaker than polylogarithmic. For example, exp(√log n) grows more slowly than every fixed positive power of n but faster than every fixed power of log n. Thus a statement of n^{o(1)} update time does not automatically meet this card’s bound. The 2020 deterministic theorem resolves an earlier polynomial-exponent barrier while leaving the sharper target.

The SODA 2026 connectivity result of Meierhans and Probst Gutenberg achieves expected polylogarithmic worst-case updates for maintaining an unweighted spanning forest, and also discusses conversion to high-probability time bounds. It extends to a (1+ε)-approximate weighted minimum spanning forest with overhead proportional to log(U)/ε for weights in [1,U]. The approximation parameter is essential; this is not an exact weighted minimum-forest theorem.

For integer weights, one could force an approximation guarantee to become exact by taking ε smaller than the reciprocal of a polynomial upper bound on the optimum cost. But the displayed 1/ε overhead would then become polynomial in n. The straightforward reduction therefore does not preserve polylogarithmic update time for exact optimization. It identifies a concrete gap between maintaining connectivity at a few approximate weight thresholds and identifying the exact cheapest replacement edge.

The oblivious-adversary convention means the update sequence is chosen without reacting to the data structure’s random outcomes. A solution robust to an adaptive adversary would be stronger. Even this stated convention would remove a longstanding delay barrier for a central dynamic optimization primitive, with uses in algorithms that repeatedly maintain weighted spanning structures.

cards.title: Polylogarithmic maintenance of the exact global minimum cut
cards.formal: Can a fully dynamic simple, unweighted, undirected n-vertex graph maintain its exact global minimum-cut value with expected polylog(n) amortized update time, worst-case polylog(n) query time and polynomial space, with high probability over every polynomial-length oblivious operation sequence?
cards.definitions: Fix vertices [n], n≥2. Start from the empty graph. A legal update inserts one absent unordered edge or deletes one present edge; there are no loops, parallel edges, weights or vertex updates. A query returns the integer λ(G)=min{ |{uv∈E:u∈S,v∉S}| : ∅≠S⊊[n] }. In particular λ(G)=0 for a disconnected graph; no distinguished terminals are supplied. Only the value is required, not a list of vertices or edges realizing the cut. Use a uniform randomized word-RAM with Θ(log(n+2))-bit words, ordinary arithmetic, bit operations and random access, and count all maintenance and query work. Precisely, ask for fixed exponents b,c and an algorithm accepting any fixed constant a≥1 as a confidence parameter. For every legal sequence with U updates and Q queries, U+Q≤n^a, fixed independently of its random bits, it uses O_a(n^b) words on every execution; expected total initialization and update work is O_a(n^b+U log^c(n+2)); each query takes O_a(log^c(n+2)) worst-case time; and all query answers are simultaneously correct with probability at least 1−n^(−3). Initial preprocessing may take O_a(n^b) time, accounting for the additive term. Each operation must finish before the next is revealed. The exponents are independent of λ(G), n and a. This fixes an expected-amortized Monte Carlo convention explicitly; it does not demand correctness against updates chosen from the random internal state.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a data structure satisfying the complete specification for unrestricted cut values, or prove that no such data structure exists in the stated model. Conditional lower bounds must state their assumptions. Algorithms for insertion-only sequences, approximate cut values, bounded connectivity or subpolynomial but superpolylogarithmic update time are partial progress. Hardness for weighted cuts or fixed-terminal s–t cuts alone is not a negative resolution.
cards.why: A central exact dynamic graph problem asking whether a global measure of edge connectivity can be updated as efficiently as basic connectivity, across the full range of cut values.

importance.reason: A fundamental data-structure question with a persistent gap between incremental, approximate and exact fully dynamic algorithms; common terminal-cut lower bounds do not settle it.

El-Hayek–Henzinger–Li obtain (1+o(1))-approximate fully dynamic minimum cut in subpolynomial amortized time.
El-Hayek–Henzinger–Li obtain deterministic exact subpolynomial amortized updates for superpolylogarithmic, but still restricted, cut sizes.
The final Algorithmica version of de Vos–Christiansen gives improved deterministic exact update bounds for unrestricted simple graphs, including Õ(m^(11/12)).

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No exact fully dynamic algorithm meeting the polylogarithmic bounds at unrestricted connectivity was found in the checked primary sources. The 2026 exact n^{o(1)} result has a cut-size restriction, and the unrestricted 2026 tree-packing bound remains polynomial rather than polylogarithmic.

context_blocks.text: The global minimum cut measures the weakest separation anywhere in a network: how many edges must fail before some nonempty part separates from the rest. Maintaining this number as individual links appear and disappear is a natural extension of dynamic connectivity. Connectivity only distinguishes λ=0 from λ≥1; the present question requires the exact integer throughout its full range from zero to n−1.

A small update need not make the identity of the best cut easy to maintain. For example, two dense clusters joined by a few edges have a global cut determined by their interface, although every individual vertex can have high degree. As the interface changes, an unrelated part of the graph can become the weakest separation. Tracking vertex degrees alone therefore does not identify the optimum.

The value changes by at most one after a single edge insertion or deletion: each individual cut changes by at most one, and taking the minimum preserves that bound. This simple stability is useful, but it does not tell an algorithm whether the answer actually changed. Certifying that no alternative cut is smaller is the difficult global part of an update.

The card requests a number, allowing a polylogarithmic query bound without an output-size obstruction. Listing the edges of a large minimum cut or all vertices on one side can require linear time merely to write the answer. It also uses the ordinary global convention λ=0 for disconnected graphs. The inherited 2026 algorithm uses minimum proper, nonzero cuts internally; those intermediate objects are not the definition of this card’s output.

Henzinger, Krinninger, Nanongkai and Saranurak’s OMv paper explicitly identifies dynamic minimum cut as an unresolved frontier for polylogarithmic updates. Its many conditional lower bounds do not automatically transfer to this task. A minimum s–t cut must separate prescribed terminals, whereas a global minimum cut may isolate a completely different region. A reduction has to preserve that freedom, not silently introduce terminal constraints.

The update model is also decisive. Goranci, Henzinger and Thorup obtained deterministic polylogarithmic amortized update time and constant query time for exact incremental minimum cut. In that setting edges are only inserted. Deletions can invalidate the compressed structural information retained during a monotone growth process, so this theorem does not settle fully dynamic maintenance.

For unrestricted cut values in simple graphs, Goranci and coauthors obtained exact fully dynamic algorithms with roughly linear-in-n randomized worst-case update time and sublinear-in-m deterministic amortized update time. Their 2024 revision corrects a runtime in the expander-decomposition analysis. This establishes substantial reuse across updates without reaching a polylogarithmic bound.

De Vos and Christiansen improve the deterministic amortized bound to Õ(m^(11/12)); their final 2026 theorem gives the more detailed minimum of m^(11/12), m^(11/13)n^(1/13), and n^(3/2), up to logarithmic factors. Their analysis uses greedy tree packings: either a packed tree crosses a minimum cut only once, or a suitable contraction exposes a minimum cut around one vertex. Both structural outcomes help reduce the candidate cuts that must be maintained.

The inherited SODA 2026 paper of El-Hayek, Henzinger and Li reaches n^{o(1)} deterministic amortized update time for exact cuts of size up to 2^{Θ((log n)^(3/4−η))}, for fixed 0<η<3/4 in the stated parameter regime. This greatly expands the previous small-cut range. It still restricts the minimum-cut value, and n^{o(1)} does not itself mean a fixed power of log n.

The same paper explains the accuracy barrier behind this restriction. Its recursive procedure controls a very small multiplicative approximation error, allowing exact recovery while the integral cut value stays below the inverse error. Making that error much smaller increases the work propagated between recursive levels. Thus simply substituting a large cut value into the theorem does not preserve its running time.

Approximation has progressed separately. El-Hayek, Henzinger and Li’s SODA 2025 algorithm maintains a (1+o(1))-approximate global cut in subpolynomial amortized time without a small-cut promise. For an integer optimum λ, rounding a multiplicative estimate to an exact answer generally needs additive error below one, hence relative error on the order of 1/λ. A fixed approximation guarantee cannot supply this for arbitrary connectivity.

The remaining question isolates two bottlenecks at once: exactness for unrestricted connectivity and polylogarithmic update cost. Randomization and amortization are allowed to make it a broad algorithmic target. A positive result would put a numerical global resilience measure close to the cost of maintaining basic connectivity, while a suitable lower bound would explain why this more detailed information requires fundamentally more work.

cards.title: Can exact fully dynamic APSP have edge-linear amortized updates and polylogarithmic queries?
cards.formal: For every fixed positive integer c, do there exist a deterministic data structure and constants a,d >= 1 such that the following holds for all n >= 2 and $n\le m\le n^2$? Maintain a directed simple graph on a fixed set of n vertices, with at most m edges at every time and integer edge weights in {1,...,n^c}, under single-edge insertions, deletions, and weight changes. Return the exact current distance from any queried vertex s to any queried vertex t in $O(\log^a n)$ worst-case time. After $O(n^d)$ preprocessing, require $O(m\log^a n)$ amortized time per update and polynomial space. Constants may depend on c, but not on n, m, the initial graph, or the operation sequence.
cards.definitions: The capacity m is supplied in advance and bounds the maximum number of live edges throughout the sequence; it is not a count of all updates. Each ordered vertex pair has at most one edge and there are no self-loops. An insertion adds an absent edge, a deletion removes a present edge, and a weight change replaces the weight of one present edge by another permitted weight. A distance query returns the minimum sum of edge weights on a directed s-to-t path, zero for s=t, and a distinguished infinity value if no path exists. Only the distance is requested, not every path or the whole distance matrix. All answers must be exact for any interleaving of updates and queries. Use a word RAM with Theta(log n)-bit words, with a sufficiently large constant for the fixed weight exponent and polynomially bounded addresses; comparisons, arithmetic, Boolean operations, shifts, and random access cost one step. Amortization means that after preprocessing any U updates and Q queries together cost $O(U m\log^a n+Q\log^a n)$; the query bound must also hold for each query individually.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a data structure with these guarantees for every fixed polynomial weight bound, or prove that the quantified proposition is false. A conditional lower bound must state its assumption. A near-quadratic-in-n update bound only meets the target for dense graphs; a subpolynomial approximation ratio or a guarantee only for insertions does not meet the exact fully dynamic specification.
cards.why: This asks whether exact shortest-path information can be maintained at a cost reflecting the number of input edges, rather than all possible vertex pairs. It is a central dynamic-graph trade-off between update work, sparse structure, and immediate exact access to global information.

importance.reason: A broad exact dynamic-graph frontier with a major sparse-versus-dense gap. It tests whether global metric information can be maintained at input-scale update cost while preserving fast queries.

progress.text: Demetrescu and Italiano give deterministic O(n^2 log^3 n) amortized updates and constant worst-case distance queries for general directed nonnegative-weight graphs.

Henzinger asks for fully dynamic APSP with edge-linear update cost and constant query cost, both allowing polylogarithmic factors. The fixed weight, edge-update, and amortization conventions here make that direction precise.
Mao’s revised paper gives a Monte Carlo algorithm with tilde-O(n^(5/2)) worst-case vertex-update time and near-quadratic space. This addresses a different update guarantee.

Kyng, Meierhans, and Zöcklein use sparsification for near-linear total processing of a bounded-length update sequence with polylogarithmic queries, but their returned distances have a subpolynomial approximation factor.

cards.status_note: The edge-sensitive target is open in the 2021 source. Searches through 10 September 2026 did not locate an exact algorithm with the stated sparse update and query bounds. This is a deterministic bounded-integer-weight specialization; approximate and worst-case vertex-update results are recorded with their different guarantees.

context_blocks.text: Recomputing distances from every source after each change is expensive, while postponing the work until a query can make a single query expensive. A dynamic distance oracle tries to divide this work so that both kinds of operation remain useful. The requested update budget is roughly the size of the current graph representation, even when that graph is sparse.

A single changed edge can alter distances for quadratically many vertex pairs. That observation does not by itself rule out a fast oracle: the representation may store those changes implicitly, and the interface only asks for one pair at a time. Proving a lower bound therefore requires more than counting changed entries in a materialized distance matrix.

The classical Demetrescu–Italiano algorithm achieves O(n^2 log^3 n) amortized update time and constant distance-query time for nonnegative weights. This is already close to the proposed bound when m is quadratic in n. The substantial gap is the sparse regime, where the desired amortized update cost can be nearly a factor n smaller.

Several nearby frontiers have different guarantees. Mao’s revised 2024 result targets worst-case vertex-update time and gives a randomized bound at the n^(5/2) scale. ESA 2025 sparsification gives extremely fast dynamic approximate distances, with a growing approximation factor. Neither result establishes the exact, edge-sensitive, amortized target on this card. Fixing those distinctions is necessary when assessing progress.

cards.title: Polynomial-sample worst-case trace reconstruction
cards.formal: For every fixed deletion probability δ∈(0,1), is there a constant C_δ≥1 and K_δ≥1 such that every unknown n-bit string can be reconstructed exactly with probability at least 2/3 from at most K_δ n^{C_δ} independent deletion traces, for every n≥2?
cards.definitions: For x∈{0,1}^n, a deletion trace is generated by independently retaining each input bit with probability 1−δ and concatenating the retained bits in their original order. Let μ_{x,δ} be its probability distribution on ⋃_{k=0}^n{0,1}^k. Different traces use independent deletion masks. The estimator is given n, δ and m independent samples from μ_{x,δ}; it receives neither deletion positions nor direct access to x. Its output is an element of {0,1}^n, and success means equality to the entire original string. One estimator for the given n and δ must succeed for every x with probability at least 2/3 over the traces and any internal randomness. There is no restriction on processing time, storage, description length or computation between observations: this card asks an information-theoretic sample-complexity question. Formally, let N_δ(n) be the smallest integer m for which such an estimator exists. The target is N_δ(n)≤K_δ n^{C_δ} for every n≥2. The constants may depend on δ but not on n or x. The string is adversarially chosen and has no codebook, sparsity, separation, randomness or other structural promise. Traces are ordinary linear subsequences without cyclic shifts.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A fundamental question about how much information random subsequences preserve: can every string be identified from polynomially many observations despite completely hidden alignment?

importance.reason: A defining worst-case recovery problem for synchronization noise, linking string algorithms, information theory, statistics and complex-analytic methods.

cards.status_note: The July 2026 quasipolynomial sample theorem supersedes the saved 2025 general upper frontier but does not give polynomially many traces. The best unrestricted lower bound cited remains polynomial; circular and local-SQ bounds concern different models. Checked through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: The input is one unknown string, observed repeatedly through independent losses of symbols. A surviving output bit carries its value but loses its original index. Repetition gives more evidence about the same underlying string, so the question is how many damaged copies contain enough information for exact recovery in the worst case.

There is an immediate exponential upper bound: with probability (1−δ)^n a trace suffers no deletions and reveals the entire string. After sufficiently many samples, such a length-n trace appears with high probability. The challenge is to extract the same information from much shorter typical traces without waiting for this rare event. Their lengths are observable, so the no-deletion event is recognizable.

Lower bounds can focus on two carefully selected strings whose trace distributions are extremely close. If even this binary hypothesis test needs many samples, reconstructing an arbitrary string cannot need fewer. Chase gives a lower bound of Ω(n^{3/2}/log⁷ n) for fixed deletion probability. This is a substantial obstruction to near-linear reconstruction, but it remains polynomial and is therefore consistent with the target.

Chase’s earlier general upper bound uses exp(Õ(n^{1/5})) traces. This substantially improved previous subexponential bounds, but left a large gap above the polynomial lower bound. The saved ICALP 2025 source accurately described that frontier at publication; it is no longer the latest general sample upper bound.

Burudgunte, Valiant and Wang’s July 2026 preprint proves a quasipolynomial sample upper bound, including every fixed positive retention probability. Its theorem bounds the number of traces by exp(p^{−7/3}(log₂ n)^c) for an absolute constant c, where p=1−δ. The strategy uses global statistics involving polylogarithmically many trace positions. It improves the upper frontier considerably while still leaving a gap to a fixed polynomial in n.

The same paper explicitly separates sample complexity from running time. Maximum-likelihood reconstruction can reuse these traces while comparing exponentially many candidate strings, whereas distinguishing two supplied candidates can be implemented much faster. The quasipolynomial sample theorem does not provide quasipolynomial time for reconstructing an arbitrary unknown string. Since the current card imposes no time limit, this distinction does not weaken the sample result.

The change in statistics matters. A local statistical-query procedure learns only approximate expectations of functions inspecting a short consecutive block of trace positions. Chen and coauthors prove strong accuracy requirements for that model, nearly matching the older subexponential algorithm. Those lower bounds do not apply to unrestricted use of individual traces or to statistics involving widely separated positions. Thus the new global approach does not contradict the local-query barrier.

Structural promises can also make the problem easier. Aamand, Liu and Narayanan show that O(n log n) traces suffice, with polynomial processing time, when successive ones are separated by sufficiently many zeros and the deletion probability is a sufficiently small constant. Their definition requires polylogarithmic separation. The theorem cannot be applied to arbitrary dense strings or to every constant deletion probability without additional arguments.

Circular trace reconstruction adds an unknown cyclic shift to each observation and asks for recovery up to rotation. The 2026 circular lower bound of roughly n⁵ is consequently a theorem for a different observation model. It should not replace the linear-model lower bound in this card. Likewise, deletion-channel coding permits a chosen codebook, while the worst-case reconstruction requirement here must cover every binary string.

cards.title: Constant-factor edit-distance approximation in O(n polylog n) time
cards.formal: Do absolute constants C≥1, K>0 and d≥0 and a uniform randomized classical algorithm exist that, for every two length-n strings x,y, output an integer D satisfying ED(x,y)≤D≤C·ED(x,y) with probability at least 2/3 in at most Kn(log₂(n+2))^d time?
cards.definitions: Use the unit-cost Levenshtein distance: ED is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions transforming x into y; matching equal symbols costs zero. The input consists of n≥1 and two explicitly stored arrays x,y∈{0,…,n²+1}ⁿ. This fixes an integer alphabet whose symbols fit in O(log n) bits and includes binary and fixed finite alphabets. Computation is on a word RAM with word length B⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ for an absolute constant B, using random access, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts and word arithmetic at unit cost. The algorithm may draw independent random bits, but has no input-dependent advice, preprocessed database or oracle. All preprocessing counts toward the bound, which must hold on every execution. Success is required separately for every input pair. Output only the distance estimate; an edit script is not required. The constants C,K,d,B are fixed independently of n and the strings. There is no promise about the distance, repetitions or input distribution, and no additive error is allowed. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo 2^w, integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length w=Θ(log n) (or Θ(log N) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Determines whether a universal constant loss in accuracy makes the basic string-alignment metric computable with only polylogarithmic overhead beyond input reading.

importance.reason: A central remaining precision–runtime boundary for edit distance, distinct from the established n^{1+ε} constant-factor algorithms and from exact-computation hardness.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No O(n polylog n)-time, fixed-constant approximation for all input pairs was found in the checked primary sources. The August 2026 journal publication gives n^{1+ε} time, and the STOC 2026 approximation scheme targets a different runtime–accuracy regime.

context_blocks.text: Insertions and deletions make alignment the central difficulty. If a symbol is inserted near the start of a string, many later positions shift, even when almost all symbols are unchanged. Comparing corresponding positions can therefore report many mismatches while a short edit sequence exists. The task is to estimate the best alignment cost without inspecting the full quadratic dynamic-programming table.

For example, deleting the first symbol of an alternating binary string and reinserting it at the end produces an equal-length string with almost every position changed, but edit distance at most two. A Hamming-distance estimate can be linear in the length on this pair. This illustrates why a simple positional comparison cannot provide a universal constant-factor approximation.

The multiplicative guarantee is deliberately strict at small distances. When x=y, success requires D=0. When the true distance is one, the returned value must remain bounded by the same universal C used on arbitrarily long strings. An additive error such as n^{0.9} can be acceptable for very distant strings while being arbitrarily poor on these nearby pairs. Reading both complete strings is allowed; this is not a sublinear-query problem.

Early algorithms already showed that one could gain substantial speed by allowing larger distortion. Andoni–Onak obtain a subpolynomial approximation factor 2^{Õ(√log n)} in n^{1+o(1)} time, with a STOC 2009 precursor and a later journal version. Both quantities improve substantially on older polynomial approximations, but the factor still grows with input length.

Koucký–Saks obtain a constant-factor result for sufficiently distant pairs, with an additive n^{1−ζ} term in the general guarantee. The exponent ζ and the multiplicative constant depend on the fixed runtime parameter. Their theorem makes the missing regime explicit: the additive term cannot be absorbed into a constant times the true distance on every pair.

Andoni–Nosatzki remove that distance promise. Their Theorem 1.1 gives, for every fixed ε>0, an O(n^{1+ε})-time randomized algorithm with approximation f(1/ε). The manuscript notes doubly exponential dependence on 1/ε. Its FOCS 2020 result was revised on arXiv in July 2022 and published in SIAM Journal on Computing in August 2026. The recent publication date does not change the quantified n^{1+ε} guarantee into n times a polylogarithm.

The order of these choices is decisive. A fixed ε=0.01 gives a fixed approximation factor, but n^{0.01} eventually exceeds every fixed power of log n. Choosing ε as a function of n to force the desired runtime also changes the approximation factor and the hidden constants. The theorem does not provide the single constant C required here. This is a quantitative gap within already very fast approximation algorithms, rather than a question about whether any strongly subquadratic constant approximation exists.

Mao–Rubinstein’s STOC 2026 work improves a different part of the tradeoff. For every fixed accuracy parameter η>0, it gives a randomized (1+η)-approximation in n²/2^{log^{Ω(1)}n} time. The approximation can be arbitrarily close to exact, but the displayed speedup is over the quadratic scale, not down to n polylog n. It does not resolve this card’s constant-factor, much-faster-runtime target.

Backurs–Indyk’s SETH-based barrier concerns exact computation in strongly subquadratic time. It should not be applied indiscriminately to approximation: the known constant-factor algorithms already run in that regime. An impossibility result for the present question would need to preserve a multiplicative gap of the appropriate size while respecting the randomized model and the very small runtime overhead.

The card concerns ordinary strings and numerical estimation. Tree edit distance, distances between languages, weighted edit operations and quantum algorithms each change the problem. Likewise, an efficient nearest-neighbour data structure with substantial preprocessing does not immediately yield the stated two-string algorithm. These distinctions keep the target useful as a precise benchmark for the algorithmic complexity of a basic sequence metric.

A positive resolution would show that constant distortion suffices to reduce this alignment problem to essentially the cost of reading its input, up to logarithmic factors. Even a large universal approximation constant would settle that structural issue. Reducing the constant, producing an alignment, and obtaining practical implementations would remain meaningful subsequent goals.

The separate card TCS-7220 asks whether every fixed ε>0 permits a (1+ε)-approximation in O(n^(2−δ_ε)) time for some fixed δ_ε>0. Its near-exact guarantee does not by itself provide this card’s O(n polylog n) runtime, while this card’s unspecified constant factor does not supply arbitrary 1+ε accuracy. The user explicitly approved retaining both targets on 11 September 2026.

cards.title: A (1+ε)-approximation for edit distance in n^(1+o(1)) time
cards.formal: For every fixed rational ε∈(0,1), is there a uniform classical randomized algorithm A_ε that, on every pair of explicitly given strings of total length n≥2, outputs an integer D with ED(x,y)≤D≤(1+ε)ED(x,y) with probability at least 2/3, using worst-case time n^(1+o(1))?
cards.definitions: ED(x,y) is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions transforming x into y, with unit cost per edit and zero cost for an equal-symbol match. String symbols are integers in {0,…,n²+1}, stored in arrays, so binary and other fixed alphabets are included. Use a word RAM with w=B_ε⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ bits for a fixed sufficiently large integer B_ε; unit-cost operations are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction, multiplication modulo 2^w and integer division by a nonzero word. Larger integers require multiple charged operations. Independent fair random bits are allowed. For each fixed ε there is one algorithm A_ε, and for every rational η>0 there are constants C_{ε,η},N_{ε,η} such that every execution on every pair of total length n≥N_{ε,η} uses at most C_{ε,η} n^(1+η) operations. A_ε halts on all inputs and has a finite worst-case bound at each smaller length as well. Constants may depend on ε and η; the algorithm may depend on ε but not on η. All preprocessing and output are charged; no advice, preprocessing oracle or input distribution is supplied. Success is required separately for every input pair. cards.title: A (1+ε)-approximation for edit distance in truly subquadratic time
cards.formal: For every fixed rational ε∈(0,1), do there exist constants δ_ε∈(0,1), K_ε>0 and a uniform classical randomized algorithm A_ε such that, for every n≥1 and every pair of length-n strings x,y, A_ε runs in at most K_ε(n+2)^(2−δ_ε) time and outputs an integer D satisfying ED(x,y)≤D≤(1+ε)ED(x,y) with probability at least 2/3? ED is unit-cost Levenshtein distance in the model below.
cards.definitions: ED(x,y) is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions converting x to y; matching equal symbols costs zero. The input strings are explicitly stored arrays over {0,…,n²+1}, including binary and fixed finite alphabets. Symbols occupy O(log n) bits. Use a word RAM with word length B⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ for a fixed sufficiently large constant B, with random access, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts and word arithmetic at unit cost. The algorithm may use independent random bits but no input-dependent advice, preprocessing oracle or preprocessed database. The runtime bound includes all preprocessing and holds on every execution; success is required separately on every input pair. Output a numerical distance estimate, with no additive error and no promise on the distance or input distribution. An edit script is not required. For each fixed ε the algorithm is uniform in n and the strings; its constants and exponent saving may depend on ε. No polynomial dependence on 1/ε, common positive saving for all ε, or efficient procedure generating A_ε is required. Rational ε suffice for every positive fixed accuracy by choosing a smaller rational parameter.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed existence statement for every fixed positive accuracy, or prove that for some fixed ε>0 no randomized algorithm achieves that multiplicative guarantee in O(n^(2−δ)) time for any fixed δ>0. A result for just one constant approximation factor does not establish the universal accuracy claim. A savings factor that is subpolynomial in n, an additive approximation, or a guarantee confined to special input distributions is insufficient. A deterministic algorithm would suffice for the positive direction, but a lower bound against deterministic algorithms alone would not settle the negative direction. Any conditional lower bound must retain its explicit assumption.

context_blocks.text: Edit distance measures the cost of aligning two sequences when insertions and deletions can shift all later positions. The question asks whether a small fixed multiplicative loss permits a fixed polynomial improvement over the quadratic dynamic-programming scale on every input. Rubinstein explicitly posed this approximation-scheme question in 2018, separately from the search for a fast constant-factor approximation.

The two parameters play different roles. Choosing ε=0.01 fixes a one-percent approximation tolerance; the desired δ_ε must then remain positive as n grows. A runtime such as n²/logⁱ n, for fixed i, is n^(2−o(1)) and does not meet the target. The requirement permits the exponent improvement to become arbitrarily small as ε approaches zero. It therefore does not ask for an exact subquadratic algorithm.

Mao and Rubinstein’s STOC 2026 paper gives randomized (1+ε)-approximation for each constant ε in n²/2^{log^{Ω(1)} n} time. Theorem 6.1 supplies a multiplicative ED estimate with high probability. This is a substantial improvement beyond logarithmic shaving, but the established quasipolynomial speedup does not provide a fixed δ_ε>0. The remaining question is whether near-exact approximation can cross that fixed-exponent boundary.

Andoni and Nosatzki obtain a different tradeoff: for each fixed η>0, a constant-factor approximation in n^(1+η) time. The approximation constant depends on η and is not guaranteed to be 1+ε for an arbitrarily prescribed ε. Thus a very fast coarse estimate and a slower near-exact estimate are distinct algorithmic achievements.

The existing card TCS-6624 asks for one fixed approximation factor in O(n polylog n) time. A positive answer here would not by itself yield that running time. Conversely, the guarantee requested in TCS-6624 does not give arbitrary 1+ε accuracy. Neither displayed guarantee alone implies the other, so both cards remain separate with the user’s explicit approval.

Backurs and Indyk establish a SETH-based barrier for exact strongly subquadratic edit distance. Such an exact-computation reduction does not automatically preserve a fixed multiplicative approximation gap. In particular, the parameter ε is fixed before the input length grows; choosing ε below 1/n to force exactness is outside any fixed-ε runtime guarantee.

Multiplicative accuracy also constrains close pairs. When ED=0 a successful estimate must be zero, and when ED=1 and ε<1 an integer successful estimate must be one. An additive term that grows with n cannot be ignored for such inputs. Weighted edits, tree edit distance and guarantees for random strings each change the problem; none is substituted for the worst-case unit-cost question here.

A resolution would locate a basic accuracy–runtime boundary for sequence comparison. It would either show that every fixed relative tolerance permits a polynomial exponent saving or identify a near-exact accuracy regime with an inherent computational obstruction. This is the scientific reason for retaining the question alongside the faster, coarser approximation target.

cards.title: Does the smallest grammar problem admit a constant-factor approximation?
cards.formal: Do there exist an absolute constant C and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, for every explicit nonempty string s, outputs an acyclic context-free grammar generating exactly s whose size is at most $C g^*(s)$? There is one production per nonterminal, one designated start nonterminal, and every right-hand side is a nonempty string of terminals and nonterminals. The dependency graph on nonterminals must be acyclic. Grammar size is the sum of all right-hand-side lengths, and $g^*(s)$ is the minimum such size. The alphabet is part of the input, encoded by integer symbols in {1,...,|s|}.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove existence of one polynomial-time algorithm with some fixed approximation constant valid for all strings, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A hardness theorem conditional on P != NP should be reported with that assumption. Exact optimization and ratios tending to one are stronger targets than the constant-factor question.
cards.definitions: Expanding a nonterminal means repeatedly replacing it by its unique right-hand side. Acyclicity guarantees termination, and the start expansion must equal the input string with no extra strings generated. Each terminal or nonterminal occurrence on a right-hand side contributes one unit to size. Runtime is measured in the ordinary binary encoding of the explicit input, not the compressed output length. Constant C cannot depend on the alphabet size, string length, or optimal grammar size. Arbitrarily long right-hand sides are permitted; the size convention is not just the number of productions.
cards.why: This is a fundamental compression-versus-optimization question: can an efficient procedure recover a representation within a fixed factor of the best hierarchical description? It also supplies a benchmark for compressed-data algorithms, whose costs often depend on grammar size rather than on the original string length.

progress.text: Charikar and coauthors give an O(1+log(|s|/g*(s))) approximation and rule out approximation ratios below 8569/8568 unless P = NP.

context_blocks.text: A grammar can share repeated pieces of a string and then share larger pieces assembled from them. For example, a sequence of doubling rules represents an exponentially long run using only a linear number of rules. This makes grammar size a useful concrete measure of repetitive structure, with a finite optimum that can in principle be found by exhaustive search.

The problem is to choose the shared pieces. Two useful repeated substrings may overlap, and a locally attractive substitution can prevent a better organization at a larger scale. A method that compresses some families extremely well can therefore still have an unbounded ratio to the best grammar on other families. The proposed guarantee must cover every input, not only average compression performance.

Known approximation guarantees depend logarithmically on the ratio between the explicit string length and its optimal grammar size. Hardness rules out sufficiently accurate approximation under P != NP, but this does not exclude a coarser universal constant. The space between these two conclusions is the question on this card.

The size measure is essential. Counting productions, binary concatenations, or all right-hand-side symbols gives related but different optimization problems. Stating the measure explicitly also avoids confusing exact binary-alphabet hardness questions with the unrestricted constant-factor approximation target.

cards.title: Can LZ77 random access use linear compressed space and logarithmic query time?
cards.formal: Given the greedy LZ77 parse with z phrases of a string $S[1..N]$ over an integer alphabet of size at most N, is there a deterministic word-RAM data structure using O(z) words in total that returns S[i] for any $1\le i\le N$ in worst-case O(log N) time? Words have $\Theta(\log N)$ bits. A phrase is a new literal or a longest prefix of the unparsed suffix having an occurrence starting earlier in S; overlapping copies are allowed. Space includes the stored parse and all query-support information. The uncompressed string is unavailable at query time.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a uniform data structure meeting both bounds for every greedy LZ77 parse, or prove that no such structure exists in the stated model. Linear space measured by a larger grammar or an LZ-End parse does not meet the O(z) requirement.
cards.why: I include this because compression is most useful when a small representation remains usable for selective queries. This question asks whether an extra logarithmic storage cost is an inherent price of navigating repeated data or a consequence of converting to a more convenient representation.
cards.definitions: All asymptotic constants are universal. The model permits standard arithmetic, multiplication, shifts, bitwise operations, comparisons, and indirect addressing on a constant number of words. A copied phrase beginning at b and referring to a<b is decoded sequentially, so self-overlap is well-defined. context_blocks.text: Lempel–Ziv compression replaces a repeated block by its earlier starting position and length. This can encode a long text with few phrases, but a position inside one copied phrase may lead to another copy, and then another. Random access asks for just one character without expanding the whole text.

The challenge is not that every deeply referenced string is hard. A long run of one repeated character can be accessed immediately once its simple structure is recognized. The target must work for arbitrary mixtures of copied material, where both the reference chains and the phrase lengths vary. Any shortcuts used to navigate those chains must fit in the compressed-space budget.

Converting the parse to a balanced grammar supplies a route to fast navigation, but the grammar can be larger than the original parse by a logarithmic factor. A space bound proportional to that grammar therefore need not be linear in z. Balancing a grammar already supplied as input is a different, solved representation problem.

The July 2026 LZ-End result is close in spirit: it obtains linear space and improved polylogarithmic access for a variant that restricts copy endpoints. Its parameter counts LZ-End phrases. Since the parsing rule and the number of phrases differ, those guarantees cannot be substituted directly for the classical LZ77 target.

cards.title: Can pattern matching run in linear time in the LZ77 input size?
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, given a valid LZ77 representation of z phrases of a text T of length N and an explicit nonempty pattern P of length m, decides whether P occurs contiguously in T in O(z+m) worst-case time? Self-referencing copy phrases are allowed. Symbols are integers in $\{1,\ldots,(z+m)^c\}$ for a fixed constant c. Use a word RAM with word size $\Theta(\log(N+m+2))$, the operations specified below, and O(z+m) working words. The input is the compressed text and the explicit pattern; all preprocessing is included.
cards.answer_criterion: Give one uniform algorithm with the stated bounds for every valid input, or prove that no such algorithm exists in this model. The output is one yes/no answer. An algorithm linear in the uncompressed text length, or in a potentially larger grammar representation, does not attain this target.
cards.definitions: Each phrase is either one literal symbol or a pair (s,l) instructing the decoder to append l symbols copied sequentially from an earlier starting position s in the text. For a phrase beginning at p, require 1 <= s < p; the copied interval may overlap the phrase being produced. Phrase boundaries and references occupy O(1) words per phrase. No promise of a greedy parse is needed. The RAM has random access, comparisons, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division, and bitwise Boolean operations and shifts on a word at unit cost; arithmetic results are restricted to a word. There is no access to a separately stored decompressed text or precomputed index.
cards.why: This is a basic test of whether computation can follow the compressed input size rather than the size of the object it describes. Settling it would also clarify whether the representation gap between LZ77 and grammars creates an unavoidable algorithmic cost for a fundamental string operation.

progress.text: Gawrychowski gives deterministic O(z(1+log(N/z))+m) time for LZ-compressed occurrence detection, including self-referential parses.
Ganardi and Gawrychowski obtain O(g+m) time when the supplied text representation is a grammar of size g. This resolves the grammar-input version.
Gawrychowski asks whether the Lempel–Ziv version can be solved in time linear in compressed-text size plus pattern length.

context_blocks.text: Ordinary pattern matching scans the text and pattern in linear time. That guarantee can be too expensive for compressed input: a short sequence of copy instructions may describe a text many orders of magnitude larger than the representation. Here the algorithm only has to determine whether an occurrence exists, so a large number of matches does not force a large output.

A match can cross phrase boundaries or occur inside a repeated region. For example, a pattern may start near the end of one copied block and finish in the next. Inspecting each phrase in isolation therefore misses valid occurrences. The challenge is to summarize enough boundary and periodicity information while charging only constant total work per input phrase and pattern symbol.

Grammar compression provides an instructive comparison. Linear-time pattern matching is known when the input is a straight-line grammar, but converting an LZ77 representation to an appropriate grammar can increase its size. The existing grammar algorithm therefore does not immediately give linear time measured in z.

The 2025 seminar question explicitly retains the Lempel–Ziv target. This card fixes the decision version, permits self-references, and charges preprocessing. These choices prevent a reporting cost or an uncharged text index from changing the question.

cards.title: Constant-factor universally truthful auctions for submodular bidders
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant C≥1 and a randomized, universally truthful combinatorial-auction mechanism that, for every number n of bidders, number m of items and normalized monotone submodular valuation profile, uses polynomial communication and produces an allocation of expected social welfare at least OPT/C?
cards.definitions: There are m≥1 distinct indivisible items and n≥1 bidders. Bidder i privately knows v_i:2^[m]→Q_{≥0}, with v_i(∅)=0, v_i(S)≤v_i(T) for S⊆T, and v_i(S)+v_i(T)≥v_i(S∪T)+v_i(S∩T) for all S,T. To make communication in bits precise, a public integer B≥1 bounds the binary lengths of the numerator and positive denominator of each value. This is a bound per value, not permission to transmit the exponential table. One uniform protocol must work for every n,m,B with at most P(n,m,B) communicated bits in the worst case, for one fixed polynomial P. Arbitrary interactive messages and demand queries are allowed; all query descriptions, replies, allocations and payments count toward communication. Local computation by bidders and auctioneer is unrestricted but must terminate. An outcome consists of pairwise disjoint bundles S_1,…,S_n and rational payments p_1,…,p_n; unallocated items are allowed. Utilities are quasilinear, u_i=v_i(S_i)−p_i. There are no private budgets or distributional assumptions. Universal truthfulness means the mechanism is a report-independent distribution over deterministic dominant-strategy truthful mechanisms: for every fixed random seed r, every i, every admissible true and alternative reported type v_i,v_i′, and every v_{−i}, v_i(S_i(v_i,v_{−i};r))−p_i(v_i,v_{−i};r)≥v_i(S_i(v_i′,v_{−i};r))−p_i(v_i′,v_{−i};r). A low-communication protocol implements this outcome and payment rule on the distributed reported types. OPT=max Σ_i v_i(T_i), where the maximum is over pairwise disjoint T_i⊆[m]. The expected welfare guarantee holds for every truthful valuation profile, with expectation only over the mechanism’s randomness; C is independent of n,m,B. No additional individual-rationality or transfer-sign restriction is imposed in this formulation.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Determine whether exact truthful incentives inherently cause an unbounded loss of allocative efficiency, even when arbitrary compact communication and unlimited local optimization are available.

importance.reason: A central multi-parameter mechanism-design problem linking truthful incentives, submodular optimization, information elicitation and the communication cost of welfare approximation.

cards.status_note: The checked primary literature retains a gap between constant nontruthful welfare approximation and the general universally truthful guarantee. Theorem 2 of the SODA 2021 paper supplies O((log log m)²) for submodular bidders. The 2026 graph-auction results impose eligibility restrictions. No general constant-factor resolution found through 11 September 2026. The public per-value precision parameter makes the inherited polynomial-communication question explicit in bits.

context_blocks.text: A bidder may value several items as substitutes. For example, a coverage valuation assigns each item a set of useful features and values a bundle by the total weight of features covered at least once. Receiving an item has less marginal value when many of its features are already covered. Submodularity abstracts this diminishing-returns property without requiring the valuation to be supplied as an explicit coverage instance.

The auctioneer must allocate the items using information held by strategic bidders. Maximizing the sum of their values is the social-welfare objective; maximizing the auctioneer’s revenue would be a different problem. Payments influence what information bidders choose to provide, but are transfers and do not enter the welfare objective. Even a very poor revenue guarantee would be acceptable here if incentives and welfare met the stated requirements.

Two established results cover separate parts of the requirements. With complete reports and unrestricted resources, the Vickrey–Clarke–Groves mechanism obtains optimal welfare and truthful incentives. If incentives are omitted, submodular welfare admits constant-factor approximation from compact queries. The difficulty is combining the guarantees while avoiding communication of exponentially many bundle values. The 2026 graph-auctions paper describes this communication perspective explicitly.

Universal truthfulness is a strong use of randomization: each mechanism obtained after fixing the coins must itself make truthful reporting optimal. Truthfulness in expectation requires only that the average utility discourage lying. The distinction has mathematical force; Dobzinski and Dughmi separate the two notions in a restricted multi-unit setting. Their separation is useful background, but their multi-unit approximation scheme does not supply a mechanism for arbitrary heterogeneous submodular valuations.

A demand query offers item prices and asks a bidder to choose a bundle maximizing its value minus its total price. Sending that bundle requires only m membership bits, even when finding it takes enormous local computation. This is why allowing demand queries changes the problem substantially. The formulation deliberately measures communication: an algorithm that delegates difficult optimization to a bidder can qualify. It would need further work to become computationally efficient for that bidder.

Dobzinski’s impossibility theorem rules out universally truthful m^{1/2−ε}-approximation using polynomially many value queries, for every fixed ε>0. A value query reveals only one specified bundle’s value. The theorem is a genuine barrier in that access model, but it cannot be extended by simply treating a demand query as one more value query. A demand answer can encode the result of comparing exponentially many bundles.

Assadi and Singla reached an expected O((log log m)³) approximation using O(n) demand queries, at FOCS 2019. Assadi, Kesselheim and Singla subsequently improved the submodular guarantee to O((log log m)²), while obtaining O((log log m)³) for the broader subadditive class. These asymptotic factors grow with the number of items, despite growing very slowly.

The latter mechanism learns approximate item prices through random groups of bidders. A bidder participates in a single fixed-price auction, so its own report cannot manipulate the menu it faces. Some price-learning rounds can become the final allocation rather than merely gathering information; the analysis accounts for welfare earned in those rounds. This makes price discovery compatible with truthfulness, but leaves a loss between the learned allocation and optimal welfare.

Recent positive results for graph auctions restrict each item to a small set of eligible bidders. For example, the 2026 paper gives a truthful factor-two mechanism when each item has two eligible bidders and valuations are subadditive. This structural restriction supplies information absent in a general auction, so it does not settle the present question. A general constant-factor mechanism would show that exact incentive compatibility need not impose an unbounded welfare loss in this central communication model.

No algorithm, runtime, or restriction to rational or strictly positive values is required.

context_blocks.text: Indivisibility prevents ordinary envy-freeness even in the smallest examples. If four people all value a single good at one, whoever receives it is envied by the others. The allocation nevertheless satisfies EFX: removing that good leaves an empty bundle. EFX permits this unavoidable envy while limiting envy that survives the removal of any positively valued item. The removal is a hypothetical comparison; the actual allocation still assigns every good.

The word “any” makes the guarantee demanding. Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 4 and another bundle’s two goods at 6 and 1. Removing the 6-valued good eliminates her envy, so this pair satisfies the weaker EF1 test. Removing the 1-valued good leaves value 6, so this pair violates EFX. All comparisons use the potentially envious agent’s values, which can differ from the recipient’s.

Zero values require a convention. If an agent has value zero for her own bundle and values the goods in another bundle at 1 and 0, removing the positively valued good passes this card’s test. Requiring removal of the zero-valued good to pass as well would fail. That stronger condition on an individual allocation is often called EFX₀. The problem statement retains the survey’s positive-good EFX convention.

For three additive agents, Chaudhury, Garg and Mehlhorn prove complete EFX existence for any number of goods. Thus the universal question starts at four agents; it is the unrestricted number of goods at that first unresolved agent count that already presents a difficulty.

The four-agent theorem of Berger, Cohen, Feldman and Fiat leaves at most one good unassigned. Completeness matters: adding that final good can create new envy, so an almost complete allocation does not itself answer the stated question.

In August 2026, Alkassar, Fouz and Mehlhorn reported complete EFX₀ existence for four agents and at most nine goods, allowing arbitrary nonnegative real values. Their theorem uses reductions and a computational certificate corpus. EFX₀ implies the EFX condition here, but the bounded number of goods leaves the unrestricted target open. The theorem’s stated scope was checked; its computations were not rerun.

Recent nonexistence results concern broader valuation classes. Mackenzie and Suzuki give counterexamples with submodular and subadditive valuations, where the value of a bundle need not equal the sum of its individual goods’ values. Such examples do not meet the additive hypothesis on this card. Likewise, a chores result concerns unwanted items and a different fairness comparison.

The issue is existence for every input valuation matrix, without an efficiency requirement. An affirmative theorem would guarantee a complete allocation with this strong relaxation of envy-freeness. A negative answer needs one additive instance in the stated domain for which every complete partition fails; finding a poor allocation or a failing allocation algorithm is insufficient.

cards.title: A constant-factor approximation for general Santa Claus allocation
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: Is there a universal constant C≥1 and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that allocates indivisible items with arbitrary nonnegative additive agent-specific values so that, with probability at least 2/3, every agent receives total value at least OPT/C, where OPT is the largest achievable minimum agent value?
cards.definitions: An input consists of n≥1 agents, m≥1 items and an explicit n×m matrix (v_ij) of nonnegative rational values, encoded by binary numerators and positive binary denominators. Agent i values a bundle S⊆[m] at v_i(S)=Σ_{j∈S}v_ij. An allocation is a tuple of pairwise disjoint bundles (S_1,…,S_n); unallocated items are permitted. Its value is F(S_1,…,S_n)=min_{i∈[n]}v_i(S_i), and OPT is the maximum of F over all allocations. Let L be the total input bit length. There must be one algorithm, one C independent of n,m and all numerical values, and one polynomial P such that the algorithm always outputs a feasible allocation within P(L) bit operations, for every random tape, and Pr[F≥OPT/C]≥2/3 on every input. The probability refers only to the algorithm’s independent internal random bits and requires the guarantee for all agents simultaneously. A deterministic algorithm is allowed as a special case. Zero values and OPT=0 are allowed, and no positive lower bound on OPT is supplied. The input values are used as given: one may not rescale each agent separately without changing the optimization problem. No identical-valuation, restricted-assignment, bounded-number-of-agents, bounded-number-of-values or bounded-item-degree assumption is imposed. All values are available to a centralized algorithm; incentives, payments and valuation oracles are not part of this problem.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a polynomial-time algorithm achieving the stated guarantee for some fixed C, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Hardness results conditional on a complexity assumption must identify that assumption, including the distinction between deterministic and randomized algorithms. A factor depending on the number of items or agents, a quasi-polynomial-time constant approximation, an estimate without an allocation, or an expected-value guarantee separately for each agent does not meet the target.
cards.why: The central unresolved max-min allocation question: can all agents be protected to within a constant factor when indivisible resources have arbitrary heterogeneous additive values?

importance.reason: A major approximation barrier in fair allocation and scheduling, linked by reductions to beating two for unrelated makespan and by relaxation gaps to the limits of fractional methods.
