context_blocks.text: A knowledge base describes incomplete information about a world. Its assertions name some objects, while its general axioms can require additional unnamed objects in every possible world. A Boolean query asks whether a finite relational pattern must exist. The problem is to decide whether the pattern follows from the whole specification, rather than whether it can be found among explicitly stored facts.

For example, let K assert Person(a) and Person⊑∃knows.Person. Every model then contains a person who knows a person, so K entails ∃x∃y(Person(x)∧knows(x,y)∧Person(y)). No named witness for y is needed. The same individual may serve as both variables when the model permits it. More complicated queries reuse variables across several edges, requiring a single assignment that satisfies all joins simultaneously.

SROIQ combines concept negation, existential and universal restrictions, singleton concepts, inverse roles, counting and regular role chains. This expressive combination underlies the logical core of OWL 2 DL. The role restrictions in the definitions are substantive: removing regularity or allowing arbitrary counting over composite roles produces different logics. The original SROIQ paper supplies a decision procedure for consistency, but that alone does not answer arbitrary conjunctive queries.

The conjunction of K with ¬q is inconsistent exactly when K entails q, but the negation of an arbitrary joined relational pattern need not be expressible as a SROIQ knowledge base. Likewise, a finite graph built by a consistency tableau is usually a compact representation of models, not an ordinary database on which evaluating q automatically gives the right answer. Unfolding repeated nodes can change whether a query cycle exists.

Rudolph and Glimm resolved a major part of the surrounding question in 2010. They handle nominals, inverse roles and counting together, and obtain decidability for SROIQ when all binary query predicates are simple roles. Thus the mere presence of those three constructors is not the remaining obstacle. The full question on this card also allows the query to inspect roles affected by transitivity and more general role compositions.

A different positive frontier comes from Horn restrictions. Ortiz, Rudolph and Šimkus show decidability even for a stronger path-query language over Horn-SROIQ, with doubly exponential combined complexity. Horn knowledge bases exclude forms of disjunctive choice that full SROIQ permits. Their result is therefore highly relevant progress, while leaving the unrestricted combination of knowledge-base features and query joins unresolved.

The distinction between all models and finite models is particularly consequential. Rudolph proves undecidability of finite conjunctive-query entailment already in a fragment of SROIQ. This is not an undecidability proof for the semantics chosen here: the sets of countermodels differ, and the distinction can affect the answer even on a small example.

To see the difference directly, require every domain element to have exactly one r-successor and at most one r-predecessor, and require a named element a to have no predecessor. The role r can be simple. Such a knowledge base has an infinite model, the natural-number successor chain, but no finite model: on a finite set, an injective total successor function would be surjective. A fresh predicate A may be empty in the infinite model, so ∃x A(x) is not entailed over all models. Over finite models it is vacuously entailed, because there are none.

Steigmiller and Glimm’s 2019 absorption method addresses practical entailment checking in very expressive logics and is implemented in Konclude. Its termination argument depends on a bounded supply of newly generated nominals in the difficult feature combination. Useful empirical behavior and termination on substantial fragments do not establish a total procedure for every SROIQ input. This conditional termination is exactly why the inherited source continues to present full decidability as open.

There is relevant progress as recently as 2026, but on a different slice of the language. Ibáñez-García, Jung, Michielini and Murlak show that conjunctive-query entailment for S, which adds transitive roles to ALC, is 2ExpTime-complete; hardness already uses two transitive roles and a Boolean conjunctive query. Their May 2026 full version also treats restrictions giving smaller upper bounds. This settles a complexity question for S, not the decidability of full SROIQ.

A positive solution would establish that general finite query patterns can always be answered against this expressive ontology language in principle. A negative solution would identify a sharp gap between consistency checking and pattern entailment inside a standard logical framework. Either outcome would clarify which expressive features can be combined while retaining an algorithmic foundation for querying incomplete knowledge.

cards.title: Does choiceless polynomial time with counting capture PTIME?
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal: Is every isomorphism-invariant polynomial-time property of finite relational structures definable in choiceless polynomial time with counting?
cards.definitions: The input is a finite structure over a fixed finite relational vocabulary, without a supplied linear order. Invariance means that relabeling its elements preserves the property. PTIME is measured on explicit relational encodings; the machine deciding a property may use the encoding order, but its answer must be invariant. The intended choiceless model operates on hereditarily finite sets built from input atoms, with counting and polynomial bounds on the active objects and execution time. No arbitrary selection of a representative from an unordered set is available.

context_blocks.text: Capturing polynomial time without relying on an arbitrary input order is a central problem of descriptive complexity. Choiceless computation is a concrete candidate formalism rather than an unspecified future logic.

Blass, Gurevich and Shelah introduce the model and analyze limits of computation without choices. Adding counting is part of this candidate’s target; negative results for the version without counting do not settle it. Particular graph families likewise do not establish capture on all finite structures.

cards.title: Is containment of conjunctive queries under bag semantics decidable?
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal: Does a Turing machine exist that halts on every pair of finite conjunctive queries q_1 and q_2 with the same output arity and decides whether $q_1(D)(a)\le q_2(D)(a)$ for every finite bag database D over their common relational signature and every output tuple a? A query $q(x)\!:\!-A_1,\ldots,A_m$ is evaluated by $q(D)(a)=\sum_{h:h(x)=a}\prod_{j=1}^{m}D(A_j[h])$, where h ranges over assignments of its variables to the finite database domain and D(A_j[h]) is the nonnegative integer multiplicity of the instantiated tuple. Both input relations and query answers retain multiplicities.
cards.definitions: A relational signature lists finitely many relation names and their arities. A finite bag database supplies a finite domain U and, for each relation symbol of arity r, a function U^r to the nonnegative integers. Zero means the tuple is absent. A query body is a finite list of positive relational atoms with variables or named constants as arguments; constants denote distinct fixed elements of U. Every variable, including every output variable, must occur in a body atom. Repeated occurrences of relation names, variables, or entire atoms are allowed and are interpreted by the displayed sum-product rule. Assignments fix constants. No disjunction, negation, inequality, comparison predicate, aggregation operator, or recursion is permitted. The output tuple lists the values of the head variables in order. Boolean queries have an empty head and return the multiplicity of the single empty tuple. The question is about deciding containment from the queries alone, with no database supplied and no size or multiplicity bound on databases.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a total algorithm deciding exactly this universal multiplicity inequality, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Enumerating counterexample databases only semidecides noncontainment. A procedure for set-valued databases, query equivalence, or a proper subclass of queries is insufficient; undecidability for unions, inequalities, or a modified numerical comparison is insufficient unless reduced to the stated plain-CQ problem.
cards.why: Bag semantics captures duplicate-sensitive query behavior, and containment is a basic correctness test for query optimization. Its unknown decidability marks a fundamental gap between simple positive query syntax and unbounded counting over finite structures. The problem also connects database theory with homomorphism inequalities and arithmetic decision problems.

importance.reason: A longstanding central decidability question for the most basic duplicate-sensitive query language. It has broad consequences for query rewriting and connects finite-model counting with undecidability boundaries.

progress.text: Chaudhuri and Vardi raise the bag-containment decidability question; the 2025 seminar traces the problem to their PODS paper.

Marcinkowski and Orda prove undecidability for nearby generalizations, including comparison after a supplied linear transformation of a Boolean query’s count. This is not the unmodified containment predicate.
Konstantinidis and Mogavero prove decidability when the left query is join-on-free and the right query is a general CQ. This extends the earlier projection-free decidable case.
The revised Marcinkowski–Ostropolski-Nalewaja paper develops techniques connecting CQ and UCQ containment, while explicitly leaving ordinary CQ-versus-CQ bag-containment decidability open.
Amarilli’s maintained question list continues to list bag-containment decidability. Current searches did not locate a resolution of the plain two-CQ formulation.

context_blocks.text: Containment asks whether one query can ever produce more of some answer than another. Under set semantics only presence matters. Under bag semantics, a join multiplies available copies and projection adds contributions from different witnesses. The multiplicities can therefore change even when the two queries return exactly the same set of answers.

For a minimal example, let q(x) have body R(x), and let r(x) have body R(x),R(x). If R(a) has multiplicity m, then q returns m copies of a and r returns m^2. Their answer sets always coincide, but the reverse bag-containment r contained in q fails as soon as m=2. This demonstrates why duplicate-insensitive rewrites need a different correctness argument.

For one fixed finite database, both values can be computed by enumerating assignments. The challenge is the quantifier over every database of every size and every choice of multiplicities. Noncontainment has a finite witness that can eventually be found by exhaustive enumeration. A decision procedure also needs to halt when no witness exists; a counterexample search by itself does not solve that side.

The 2025 seminar still identifies this as a longstanding unresolved boundary. Recent work establishes decidability for a restricted left-hand query in which existential variables do not participate in joins, while related work proves undecidability after extending the query language or numerical comparison. These results make the precise boundary especially significant: small changes around the basic formulation have known answers, but do not settle two unrestricted plain conjunctive queries.

cards.title: Does naive evaluation over p-stable semirings converge in O((p+1)n) rounds?
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal: Is there a universal constant C such that the following holds for every integer p>=0, every n>=1, every commutative p-stable semiring S, and every polynomial map F:S^n -> S^n with coefficients in S? Starting with x^(0)=(0,...,0), perform synchronous iteration x^(t+1)=F(x^(t)). There must exist an integer t<=C(p+1)n with x^(t+1)=x^(t). Here p-stability means $1\oplus a\oplus\cdots\oplus a^p=1\oplus a\oplus\cdots\oplus a^{p+1}$ for every a in S. The constant C is independent of the semiring, coefficients, number of monomials, and polynomial degrees. This is the grounded polynomial-system formulation of the source’s proposed linear convergence bound.
cards.definitions: A commutative semiring has associative, commutative addition op-plus with identity 0 and associative, commutative multiplication op-times with identity 1. Multiplication distributes over addition, and 0 times a=0. No additive inverses are assumed. Powers use semiring multiplication and a^0=1. Every component of F is a finite sum of finite products of coefficients and variables; repeated variables and constant terms are allowed. S need not be finite. One round evaluates all components using only the previous vector, not partially updated coordinates. Equality means exact equality of semiring elements. The cost measure is the number of rounds, irrespective of the work needed to evaluate a component or represent an element. In a grounded Datalog program, coordinates represent individual derived facts and their values are annotations; using all n coordinates also includes any that remain zero.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal bound, or refute it by constructing systems whose first fixed-point time divided by (p+1)n is unbounded. A fixed example exceeding n rounds does not refute an unspecified constant C. A bound with a growing factor depending on degrees, coefficients, or n does not establish this target. A faster evaluation algorithm with a different update rule does not by itself bound the number of synchronous naive iterations.
cards.why: The problem asks whether local algebraic stability imposes a sharp global limit on recursive evaluation. A universal linear bound would explain why a broad class of annotated recursive computations needs only an output-scale number of rounds, while a separation would expose a fundamental cost of nonlinear interactions.

importance.reason: A foundational convergence question for semiring-valued recursion, with implications beyond one query language. Its historical significance is high, but a newly announced directly relevant paper makes current open status uncertain.

progress.text: Work on convergence of Datalog over pre-semirings establishes stable-semiring convergence and an exponential upper bound in the number of grounded coordinates; the later polynomial paper reviews this starting point.
Im, Moseley, Ngo, and Pruhs establish polynomial convergence for nonlinear programs. The inspected arXiv v2 states the additional sigma and lambda dependencies explicitly.
Ngo records the gap between the polynomial upper bound and Omega((p+1)n), and proposes a matching linear upper bound.

context_blocks.text: In ordinary Boolean Datalog, a derived fact switches from absent to present at most once. A nonstationary round must add a fact, so the number of possible facts bounds the number of rounds. Annotated recursion can improve the value attached to an already known fact many times. Counting how many coordinates exist therefore ceases to give an immediate termination bound.

The stability assumption controls repeated use of a single semiring element. It says that a sufficiently long truncated geometric sum absorbs the next power. The question asks whether a system of n interacting recurrences can multiply the resulting delay by only O(n), even when the equations are nonlinear. This is a structural claim about composition of recursive dependencies, not a bound on the time taken by one database join.

The examined Im–Moseley–Ngo–Pruhs preprint proves a polynomial convergence bound, with explicit dependence on sigma, the number of distinct coefficients referenced, and lambda, the maximum number of multiplicands. Its bound is O(sigma p n^2 (n^2 log(lambda+1)+log(sigma+1))) for positive p; the 0-stable case has a separate linear bound. Suppressing sigma and lambda would conceal part of the remaining challenge.

The 2025 seminar asks for O((p+1)n), matching the order of its stated lower bound. A newer paper titled Optimal Convergence of Iterative Methods for Datalogo is now listed by its authors. The inspected listings supply no theorem or accessible manuscript for that entry. This card therefore preserves the precise historical question with an uncertain current status; the title alone does not identify which convergence bound, iteration scheme, or semiring hypotheses it settles.

cards.definitions: [n]={1,…,n}. A partial order ≤_P is a reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive relation. Distinct x,y are incomparable when neither x≤_P y nor y≤_P x; P is a total order when no such pair exists. A linear extension is a bijection L:[n]→[n] with L(a)<L(b) whenever a≤_P b and a≠b. Let E(P) be the finite nonempty set of all linear extensions, e(P)=|E(P)|, and e_P(x,y)=|{L∈E(P):L(x)<L(y)}|. Equivalently choose L uniformly from E(P), so the displayed interval requires Pr[L(x)<L(y)]∈[1/3,2/3], including endpoints. The pair x,y may depend on the entire poset. This is an existence proposition over all finite orders, with no width, height or representation restriction and no algorithmic requirement. Width is the largest size of a set of pairwise incomparable elements; height is the largest size of a totally ordered subset. For context, the balance constant is β(P)=max_{x≠y} min{e_P(x,y),e_P(y,x)}/e(P); this card uses β to avoid conflicting δ conventions across sources.

context_blocks.text: A partial order records comparisons already known, and its linear extensions are all complete rankings still compatible with that information. The conjecture says that unless only one ranking remains, some unresolved comparison splits these possible rankings into two substantial groups. Neither outcome may leave more than two thirds of them. The distribution is uniform over whole rankings, not over the currently available choices in a stepwise topological sort.

Take three elements with a<b and c unrelated to both. The three linear extensions are abc, acb and cab. The probability that a precedes c is 2/3, while the probability that b precedes c is 1/3. No incomparable pair is closer to a half. This small example shows that the universal interval cannot be narrowed to [1/3+η,2/3−η] for any η>0. In a total order every pair instead has probability zero or one, which explains the excluded case.

Uniform local choices need not produce uniform extensions. In the same example, choosing randomly between the two initially minimal elements a and c gives cab probability 1/2, and gives abc and acb probability 1/4 each. Those are different from the required probabilities 1/3 each. Fixing the probability space prevents a superficially similar random-ordering question from replacing the conjecture.

Brightwell, Felsner and Trotter prove the weaker universal bound β(P)≥(5−√5)/10≈0.2764. It already guarantees an informative comparison and improves the earlier 3/11 bound of Kahn and Saks. The requested value 1/3 is a sharper extremal constant, rather than the first guarantee of any fixed positive balance.

The conjecture is known for substantial classes, including width-two and height-two orders, and orders whose cover graph is a forest. Width limits how many elements can be mutually incomparable; height limits the length of a chain. These are distinct restrictions, and neither covers arbitrary finite orders. The Chan–Pak survey states the general question separately from this collection of positive cases.

Aires and Kahn obtain stronger asymptotic balance under size hypotheses: for example β(P) tends to 1/2 when width is at least a fixed positive fraction of the number of elements. Their 2025 paper still states the unrestricted 1/3–2/3 bound as a conjecture. A result for a sequence of sufficiently wide orders leaves narrower and exceptional finite orders uncovered.

Gupta’s July 2026 revision reports an exhaustive verification of the stronger Gold Partition property through fourteen elements, implying the balance conjecture for those sizes. Its arithmetic and archived artifacts are described in the paper; this review did not rerun the census. A verified finite range, however large its enumeration, does not establish the universal statement.

cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed inequalities for at least one incomparable pair in every finite non-total order, or exhibit a finite non-total order for which every incomparable pair has probability outside [1/3,2/3]. All probabilities refer to the uniform distribution on its full set of linear extensions.

cards.definitions: For n≥1, S_n is the set of permutations π=(π₁,…,π_n) of [n]={1,…,n}. For 2≤j≤n, a prefix reversal r_j sends π to (π_j,π_{j−1},…,π₁,π_{j+1},…,π_n). Each reversal costs one, regardless of j. Let d_n(π) be the least length of a finite reversal sequence sending π to (1,…,n), with the empty sequence allowed. Define f(n)=max_{π∈S_n}d_n(π); thus f(1)=0. Reversals generate S_n, so all these minima and maxima are finite. Equivalently f(n) is the diameter of the undirected Cayley graph on S_n with these prefix reversals. This is the unsigned, or unburnt, problem: no signs or orientations are tracked. Suffix reversals, arbitrary interval reversals and repeated symbols are not permitted. The remaining ambiguity concerns what general description of f is required as an answer, not the definition of f itself.

context_blocks.text: A stack is represented from top to bottom by a permutation of pancake sizes. The spatula can turn over an initial segment, so one move changes the order of several entries but always includes the top. The pancake number is the worst possible optimal flip count at a given stack size. It measures the power of this restricted operation, rather than the number of comparisons used by ordinary sorting.

For three pancakes, 132 can be sorted in three flips: 132→312→213→123, with prefix lengths 2,3,2. It cannot be sorted in two: its one-step neighbors are 312 and 231, whereas the sorted stack’s one-step neighbors are 213 and 321. These sets are disjoint. The six states can all be sorted within three moves, so f(3)=3. A flip count for one stack and a worst-case upper bound play different roles in such an equality.

Chitturi and coauthors give f(n)≤(18/11)n+O(1). Both the known lower and upper bounds are linear, but their leading coefficients remain separated. Merely proving f(n)=Θ(n) would restate an already known order of growth.

Peczarski’s 2026 note extends the lower bound to f(n)≥floor((15n+9)/14) for n≥6, improving coverage of stack sizes. The statement is given in the preprint and the author’s February exposition. It does not match the universal upper-bound coefficient.
Cibulka computed exact values through n=19, where f(19)=22. A finite table gives rigorous information about those sizes without determining the sequence at arbitrary n.

Amano’s near-(15/14)n sorting bound applies to a particular family used in lower-bound constructions, not every permutation. An upper bound on that family cannot be substituted for a universal upper bound on f.
Bulteau, Fertin and Rusu establish NP-hardness of finding the optimum for a supplied stack. That input-specific computational problem differs from describing the maximum optimum as a function of n.

Jäger and Oijid’s January 2026 result concerns the signed starting stack (−1,…,−n) and settles its optimum for an additional parity class. This is a different extremal question from the unburnt diameter defined here.

The benchmark target still needs specification. For each fixed n, the finite graph definition already permits exact computation without a runtime limit. The imported request to “determine f(n)” does not specify what must improve on that existing computation. This card records the mathematical quantity and known bounds while leaving that acceptance requirement unresolved; it does not silently replace exact determination with an asymptotic or efficient-algorithm question.

cards.title: The sunflower conjecture
cards.formal: For every integer r≥3, is there a real C_r>0 such that every family of more than C_r^k distinct k-element sets contains r members whose pairwise intersections are all equal, for every integer k≥1?
cards.definitions: The sets may lie in any finite universe. The r selected sets must be distinct. Their common pairwise intersection is called the core; removing it gives pairwise disjoint petals, which may include the empty set. C_r depends only on r, not on k, the universe or the family. No construction algorithm or bound on the universe size is required.

context_blocks.text: Sunflowers capture a simple repeated pattern inside a large family of small sets. Bounds on their forced occurrence are basic tools in circuit complexity, pseudorandomness and kernelization.

The breakthrough bound of Alweiss, Lovett, Wu and Zhang replaces a much larger dependence by roughly (log k)^{O(k)} for fixed r. The conjecture asks for a constant base to the k-th power. This is admitted as a computationally motivated exception to the exclusion of general combinatorics, not to fill a combinatorics category.

cards.definitions: A tile type is a unit square with a fixed orientation and a glue label and nonnegative integer strength on each of its four sides. A system has finitely many types, an unlimited supply of each, and a finite seed assembly on the integer square lattice whose positive-strength matching contacts form a connected graph. Matching labels on adjacent sides contribute their glue strength; other contacts contribute zero and are permitted. Starting from the seed, a step places one tile in an empty lattice cell if the total matching strength is at least 1. Tiles never rotate, detach, or change glues. Assembly choices and their order are asynchronous. Directed means that all producible assemblies are compatible with one terminal assembly, which may be infinite; directedness is not required here. Negative glues, a third spatial dimension, staged changes of tile supply, and nonsquare tiles are outside the model.

cards.title: Polylogarithmic universal reconfiguration with amoebot joint movements
cards.formal: Do a constant C>0, an integer k>=0, and a deterministic centralized scheduling algorithm exist such that, for every n>=1 and every pair of connected configurations of n contracted amoebots on the triangular lattice, the algorithm produces a legal reconfiguration from the first shape to a congruent copy of the second in at most C(1+log_2 n)^k synchronous rounds? Use the discrete geometric joint-movement model defined below. The scheduler knows both configurations and its computation time is unrestricted; the cost is the number of movement rounds. No additional particles or promise of preassembled metamodules is allowed.
cards.definitions:
Use the lattice Z^2 with neighbor vectors ±(1,0), ±(0,1), ±(1,-1), embedded as equilateral triangles. A contracted particle occupies one vertex; an expanded particle occupies two adjacent vertices and their edge. Different particles have disjoint occupied vertices. Adjacent particles initially share bonds, which are unit lattice edges. Particle edges and bonds together must form a connected graph. Particles are indistinguishable for the final shape; input shapes are finite coordinate lists. Translation, lattice rotations, and reflection of the target are allowed, as in the source's shape classes.

A round first removes chosen bonds, with at least one endpoint choosing each removal, while retaining connectivity. Each particle then performs at most one action: no action; expansion; contraction; or participation in an isolated handover with one neighbor. Expansion splits a contracted vertex into two endpoints of a new unit particle edge along a lattice axis and distributes its retained incident bonds between those endpoints without changing the bonds' oriented unit vectors. Contraction reverses such a split. Thus other particles may be displaced by attached expanding or contracting particles. In a handover, a contracted particle at u and an expanded neighbor occupying v,w exchange the roles of their connecting bond uv and particle edge vw: the former particle occupies u,v, the latter occupies w, and vw becomes a bond. Participating particles perform no other action in that round.

All simultaneous changes must yield a connected graph admitting an injective embedding in the triangular lattice with every retained bond and particle edge having its prescribed orientation and unit length. Inconsistent embeddings and two particles occupying a common vertex are forbidden. Finally, add every bond between newly adjacent particles. This is the discrete collision and connectivity convention of Section 2.1 of the 2026 source, rather than a different continuous mechanical motion model. The initial and final particles are contracted; intermediate ones may expand. One round includes both bond release and the simultaneous actions.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove or refute the existence of a single scheduler and fixed C,k satisfying this bound for all connected pairs and all n under the stated joint-movement rules.
cards.why: This asks whether programmable matter can change an arbitrary global shape in only polylogarithmically many coordinated movements. Even unlimited knowledge and planning leave a geometric constraint, so the answer would identify a physical reconfiguration barrier distinct from local communication delay.

importance.reason: A universal shape-change speed limit in a basic model of programmable matter, rather than an optimization for one robot shape.
